description: From electronics and Arduino firmware through sensors, actuators, control, kinematics, perception, planning and ROS 2 to robot learning and VLA foundation models. A self-study path for building robots and following Physical AI.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::01 Electronics Fundamentals
notes.text: Ohm's law: {{c1::V = I·R}}. Electrical power: {{c2::P = V·I = I²·R = V²/R}}.
notes.extra: Robotics use: sizing resistors, wire gauge, regulator heat, battery current.
notes.source: Horowitz & Hill, The Art of Electronics (3rd ed.)

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::01 Electronics Fundamentals
notes.front: Voltage divider: output formula?
notes.back: V<sub>out</sub> = V<sub>in</sub> · R2 / (R1 + R2)
notes.extra: Example: R1 = 1 kΩ, R2 = 2 kΩ scales 5 V to 3.33 V.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::01 Electronics Fundamentals
notes.front: Voltage divider on a robot: name a correct use and the classic misuse.
notes.back:
Correct: scaling a signal (5 V → 3.3 V), reading resistive sensors, battery monitoring on an analog-to-digital converter (ADC) pin.
Misuse: as a power supply; output sags as soon as a load draws current.
notes.analogy: A divider is a tap on a leaky pipe: fine for sensing pressure, useless for delivering flow.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::01 Electronics Fundamentals
notes.front: How do you size a light-emitting diode (LED) series resistor? (5 V supply, 2 V forward voltage, 10 mA)
notes.back: R = (Vsupply − Vf) / I = 3 V / 0.010 A = 300 Ω → next standard value, 330 Ω.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::01 Electronics Fundamentals
notes.front: What problem does a pull-up (or pull-down) resistor solve?
notes.back: A disconnected (floating) input picks up noise and reads randomly; a pull-up (~10 kΩ to Vcc) or pull-down (to GND) defines the idle level.
notes.analogy: A door spring: without it the door flaps in the wind; with it the door rests in a known position until someone pushes.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::01 Electronics Fundamentals
notes.front: With pinMode(pin, INPUT_PULLUP), how is a button wired and what does a press read?
notes.back: Button between pin and ground; the internal ~20–50 kΩ pull-up holds it HIGH, so a press reads LOW (active-low).

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::01 Electronics Fundamentals
notes.front: What does a decoupling (bypass) capacitor do?
notes.back: Sits between an integrated circuit (IC)'s supply pin and ground, supplying fast transient current locally and shunting high-frequency noise.
notes.analogy: A small water tank right next to the tap: sudden demand is met locally instead of waiting for the distant main.
notes.source: Horowitz & Hill, The Art of Electronics (3rd ed.)

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::01 Electronics Fundamentals
notes.front: Standard placement practice for decoupling capacitors?
notes.back: 100 nF ceramic as close as possible to every integrated circuit (IC) supply pin, plus bulk electrolytic (100–1000 µF) near motor drivers and servo rails.
notes.source: Horowitz & Hill, The Art of Electronics (3rd ed.)

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::01 Electronics Fundamentals
notes.front: Why does a relay, solenoid or brushed motor switched by a transistor need a flyback diode?
notes.back: Inductor current can't stop instantly: V = −L·di/dt makes a large spike when the switch opens, killing the transistor. A reverse-parallel diode lets the current decay.
notes.analogy: Like water hammer: slam a valve on flowing water and the pipe bursts; the diode is the relief valve.
notes.extra: Note: H-bridge driver integrated circuits (ICs) usually have these built in (or use metal-oxide-semiconductor field-effect transistor (MOSFET) body diodes).
notes.source: Horowitz & Hill, The Art of Electronics (3rd ed.)

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::01 Electronics Fundamentals
notes.front: Low-side N-channel metal-oxide-semiconductor field-effect transistor (MOSFET) switch from a microcontroller unit (MCU) pin: where do load, source and gate go?
notes.back: Load between V+ and drain; source to ground; gate driven by the pin. Load supply and MCU share a common ground.
notes.source: Horowitz & Hill, The Art of Electronics (3rd ed.)

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::01 Electronics Fundamentals
notes.front: Metal-oxide-semiconductor field-effect transistor (MOSFET) low-side switch: what does each support part do? (logic-level field-effect transistor (FET), gate resistor, gate pull-down)
notes.back:
• Logic-level FET: fully on at 3.3–5 V gate drive (RDS(on) specified at 2.5/4.5 V)
  • ~100–220 Ω gate resistor: limits gate charging current
  • ~10 kΩ gate–source pull-down: keeps it off during reset
notes.extra: Plus: flyback diode if the load is inductive.
notes.source: Horowitz & Hill, The Art of Electronics (3rd ed.)

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::01 Electronics Fundamentals
notes.front: What is the risk of feeding 5 V into a 3.3 V input (e.g. Raspberry Pi)?
notes.back: It forward-biases the pin's protection diodes and can destroy the pin (unless it is explicitly 5 V tolerant).

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::01 Electronics Fundamentals
notes.front: Level-shifting options between 5 V and 3.3 V logic?
notes.back:
• Resistor divider: one direction, slow signals
  • BSS138 metal-oxide-semiconductor field-effect transistor (MOSFET) shifter: bidirectional, ideal for inter-integrated circuit (I2C)
  • Translator integrated circuit (IC) (74LVC245, TXS0108)
notes.extra: Note: 3.3 V into a 5 V input often works but is marginal (ATmega328P needs ≥ 0.6·Vcc = 3.0 V for HIGH).

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::01 Electronics Fundamentals
notes.front: Lithium polymer (LiPo) cell voltages: nominal, full, and minimum?
notes.back: 3.7 V nominal, 4.2 V full, don't discharge below ~3.0–3.3 V.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::01 Electronics Fundamentals
notes.front: What does a lithium polymer (LiPo) labelled '3S 2200 mAh 25C' give you?
notes.back: 3S = 3 cells in series → 11.1 V nominal (12.6 V full). Max continuous current = 2.2 Ah × 25 = 55 A.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::01 Electronics Fundamentals
notes.front: How long can a 2200 mAh lithium polymer (LiPo) pack sustain its 55 A maximum continuous current?
notes.back: About 2.2 Ah ÷ 55 A = 0.04 h ≈ 2.4 minutes. The C-rating is a current limit, not a runtime.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::01 Electronics Fundamentals
notes.front: Lithium polymer (LiPo) safety rules?
notes.back: Balance-charge with a LiPo charger, use a low-voltage cutoff/alarm, never puncture or charge unattended: fire hazard.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::01 Electronics Fundamentals
notes.front: Linear regulator vs. buck converter: how do they differ?
notes.back:
Linear: burns the excess as heat, P = (Vin − Vout)·I; simple, low-noise.
Buck: switches an inductor, ~85–95% efficient, slightly noisier.
notes.analogy: A linear regulator is a brake that turns surplus speed into heat; a buck converter is a gearbox that trades voltage for current.
notes.source: Horowitz & Hill, The Art of Electronics (3rd ed.)

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::01 Electronics Fundamentals
notes.front: Why not use a linear regulator to power a Raspberry Pi from a 12 V battery?
notes.back: 12 V → 5 V at 3 A would dissipate 21 W as heat. Use a buck converter rated for the Pi's peak current (Pi 5: 5 V / 5 A).
notes.source: Horowitz & Hill, The Art of Electronics (3rd ed.)

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::01 Electronics Fundamentals
notes.front: When is a linear regulator still the better choice than a buck converter?
notes.back: For low-current, low-noise rails (sensors, analog circuits) with a small input-output difference, where the wasted heat is tiny. A common pattern: buck down near the target, then a low-dropout (LDO) regulator for a clean rail.
notes.source: Horowitz & Hill, The Art of Electronics (3rd ed.)

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::01 Electronics Fundamentals
notes.front: Why must all boards on a robot share a common ground?
notes.back: A signal voltage only means something relative to a shared 0 V; without it levels are undefined and links fail or damage pins.
notes.analogy: Two people measuring height from different floors: the numbers are meaningless until they agree where zero is.
notes.source: Horowitz & Hill, The Art of Electronics (3rd ed.)

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::01 Electronics Fundamentals
notes.front: How do you keep motor currents from corrupting logic signals?
notes.back: Star ground at the battery/regulator, heavy motor return currents on their own thick wires (not through logic ground), and local decoupling.
notes.source: Horowitz & Hill, The Art of Electronics (3rd ed.)

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::01 Electronics Fundamentals
notes.front: Symptom: the microcontroller unit (MCU) resets whenever the motors start. Cause?
notes.back: Motor inrush/stall current sags the supply below the brown-out threshold (or injects noise).

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::01 Electronics Fundamentals
notes.front: Name three fixes for a microcontroller unit (MCU) that resets when motors start, and what each protects against.
notes.back:
• Separate logic regulator/battery: isolates logic from motor supply sag
  • Bulk capacitor on the motor supply: supplies inrush current locally
  • Short, thick wiring and capacitors across brushed-motor terminals: less voltage drop and switching noise

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::01 Electronics Fundamentals
notes.front: Why must motors and servos never be powered from the Arduino 5 V pin?
notes.back: That pin is fed by the board's regulator or USB port, which supplies far less current than motor start or stall demands. The supply sags (brown-out resets) or the regulator is damaged. Use a separate supply with a common ground.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::02 Microcontrollers & Embedded Linux
notes.front: Microcontroller unit (MCU) vs. microprocessor unit (MPU): what is the difference?
notes.back:
MCU: CPU + flash + RAM + peripherals on one chip; bare-metal/RTOS; deterministic µs timing.
MPU: needs external RAM/storage, runs Linux; high throughput, non-deterministic timing.
notes.extra:
Examples: MCU: ATmega328P, STM32, ESP32, RP2040. MPU: Raspberry Pi, Jetson.
Pi limits: no analog-to-digital converter (ADC), fragile 3.3 V I/O, slow boot, needs clean shutdown.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::02 Microcontrollers & Embedded Linux
notes.front: Why can't a Raspberry Pi simply replace the Arduino on a robot?
notes.back: Linux scheduling gives timing jitter, so hard real-time I/O (motor pulse-width modulation (PWM), encoder counting, safety timeouts) belongs on a microcontroller unit (MCU). Robots pair them: microprocessor unit (MPU) for perception/planning, MCU for real-time control.
notes.analogy: The Pi is the brain planning the route; the MCU is the spinal cord handling reflexes that can't wait for a thought.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::02 Microcontrollers & Embedded Linux
notes.front: Name the four datasheet facts to check before wiring a sensor or actuator to a microcontroller unit (MCU) board, and what each prevents.
notes.back:
• Logic level (5 V or 3.3 V): damaged pins
  • Analog-to-digital converter (ADC) resolution and reference: misread values
  • Hardware pulse-width modulation (PWM) pins: jittery motor or servo control
  • External interrupt pins: missed encoder edges
notes.extra: Example, Arduino UNO R3: ATmega328P, 8-bit AVR @ 16 MHz, 5 V logic, 10-bit analog-to-digital converter (ADC), pulse-width modulation (PWM) on 3, 5, 6, 9, 10, 11, external interrupts only on pins 2 and 3; 32 KB flash · 2 KB static random-access memory (SRAM) · 1 KB electrically erasable programmable read-only memory (EEPROM).

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::02 Microcontrollers & Embedded Linux
notes.front: Moving a design to a newer, faster microcontroller unit (MCU) board: which electrical assumption most often breaks?
notes.back: Per-pin drive current (and sometimes logic level). A 32-bit board can source far less per I/O pin than an 8-bit one, so light-emitting diodes (LEDs) or transistor gates driven straight from a pin stop working. Re-check the datasheet.
notes.extra: Example: Arduino UNO R4 (Cortex-M4, 14-bit analog-to-digital converter (ADC), digital-to-analog converter (DAC), controller area network (CAN), still 5 V) allows only ~8 mA per pin vs ~20 mA on the UNO R3.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::02 Microcontrollers & Embedded Linux
notes.front: How do you convert analogRead() to volts, and what is the UNO R3 step size?
notes.back: V = reading × Vref / 2n. UNO R3: 10-bit (0–1023), 5 V/1024 ≈ 4.88 mV per step.
notes.extra: Finer resolution: more bits, or a lower reference via analogReference().

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::02 Microcontrollers & Embedded Linux
notes.front: What does analogWrite() actually output on an UNO R3?
notes.back: Not an analog voltage: a pulse-width modulation (PWM) square wave, 8-bit duty (0–255) at ~490 Hz (~980 Hz on pins 5, 6). Average = duty × 5 V.
notes.analogy: Flicking a light switch very fast: the room looks half-lit, but the bulb is only ever fully on or off.
notes.extra: Fine for light-emitting diode (LED) dimming and motor-driver inputs; needs a low-pass filter for a true analog level. UNO R4 has a real digital-to-analog converter (DAC) on A0.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::02 Microcontrollers & Embedded Linux
notes.front: Why is delay() a problem in robot code?
notes.back: It blocks the CPU: no sensor reads, no control updates, missed events.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::02 Microcontrollers & Embedded Linux
notes.front: What is the standard non-blocking timing pattern on Arduino ('blink without delay')?
notes.back: if (millis() - last >= interval) { last = millis(); task(); } — each task keeps its own timestamp, so many periodic jobs share loop().
notes.analogy: A cook glancing at several timers between tasks, instead of staring at one pot until it boils.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::02 Microcontrollers & Embedded Linux
notes.front: How do you write millis() timing that survives the ~49.7-day rollover?
notes.back: Use unsigned long and compare by subtraction: millis() - start >= interval. Never millis() >= start + interval.
notes.analogy: A clock face: from 11 to 2 is 3 hours whichever way the numbers wrap, as long as you count the gap, not compare positions.
notes.extra: Unsigned modular arithmetic keeps the difference correct across the wrap; the addition overflows.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::02 Microcontrollers & Embedded Linux
notes.front: Why does millis() - start >= interval still work when millis() rolls over?
notes.back: Unsigned arithmetic wraps modulo 232, so the subtraction still gives the true elapsed time. In millis() >= start + interval the sum itself overflows and breaks.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::02 Microcontrollers & Embedded Linux
notes.front: Arduino interrupt service routine (ISR) rules: what should (and shouldn't) happen inside an interrupt handler?
notes.back: Keep it tiny: set a flag/count, do the work in loop(). No delay(), no Serial; millis() doesn't advance inside.
notes.extra: Typical use: wheel-encoder edges. Attach with attachInterrupt(digitalPinToInterrupt(pin), isr, RISING).

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::02 Microcontrollers & Embedded Linux
notes.front: Variables shared between an interrupt service routine (ISR) and loop() on 8-bit AVR: which two precautions?
notes.back: Declare them volatile; copy multi-byte values inside noInterrupts()/interrupts(), since they aren't read atomically.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::02 Microcontrollers & Embedded Linux
notes.front: Why must a variable shared with an interrupt service routine (ISR) be volatile? What breaks otherwise?
notes.back: The compiler may keep the value in a register, so loop() never sees the ISR's update (e.g. a flag that never changes).

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::02 Microcontrollers & Embedded Linux
notes.front: What is switch bounce, and how do you debounce in software?
notes.back: Contacts chatter for ~1–20 ms, giving many edges per press. Accept a new state only after it has been stable for 20–50 ms (timed with millis()).
notes.extra: Hardware alternative: resistor-capacitor (RC) filter + Schmitt trigger.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::02 Microcontrollers & Embedded Linux
notes.front: On an UNO R3, what side effect does the Servo library have?
notes.back: It takes over Timer1, disabling analogWrite() pulse-width modulation (PWM) on pins 9 and 10.
notes.extra: Lesson: timers are shared hardware; Servo, tone, motor shields and encoder libraries can conflict.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::02 Microcontrollers & Embedded Linux
notes.front: How much current can an UNO R3 I/O pin supply, and what follows?
notes.back: ~20 mA recommended (40 mA abs. max), ~200 mA total. Never drive a motor, relay coil or servo from a pin or the 5 V pin; use a transistor/driver with its own supply.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::02 Microcontrollers & Embedded Linux
notes.front: What does a Wi-Fi/Bluetooth-capable microcontroller unit (MCU) (e.g. ESP32) add to a hobby robot?
notes.back: Wireless telemetry and tele-op on the MCU itself, a faster (often multi-core) CPU, many peripherals and a built-in real-time operating system (RTOS), usually still programmable like a plain MCU from the Arduino integrated development environment (IDE).

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::02 Microcontrollers & Embedded Linux
notes.front: Why is the ESP32's analog-to-digital converter (ADC) a weak choice for precise sensing, and what extra limit applies with Wi-Fi?
notes.back: Its response is non-linear (needs calibration or an external ADC), and the ADC2 channels cannot be used while Wi-Fi is on.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::02 Microcontrollers & Embedded Linux
notes.front: Why can enabling Wi-Fi make an ESP32 board brown-out reset, and what fixes it?
notes.back: Radio transmit bursts draw current spikes (~500 mA) that sag a weak supply below the brown-out threshold. Fix: a stiff 3.3 V regulator and a bulk plus decoupling capacitor near the module.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::02 Microcontrollers & Embedded Linux
notes.front: Which logic-level and boot-time pitfalls apply to ESP32 boards?
notes.back: 3.3 V logic, not 5 V tolerant (use a level shifter). Boot-strapping pins have reserved states at reset, so external circuits on them can stop the board from booting.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::02 Microcontrollers & Embedded Linux
notes.front: Why structure robot firmware as a Finite State Machine?
notes.back: Explicit states (IDLE, SEARCH, GRAB, FAULT) with event-triggered transitions: non-blocking, predictable, easy to debug, and an obvious place for a safe FAULT state.
notes.extra: Implementation: enum + switch inside loop().

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::02 Microcontrollers & Embedded Linux
notes.front: What does a real-time operating system (RTOS) (FreeRTOS, Zephyr) give you over a bare-metal super-loop?
notes.back: Pre-emptive, priority-based tasks with bounded latency, plus queues, mutexes/semaphores and software timers.
notes.analogy: A super-loop is one waiter serving tables in a fixed order; an RTOS is a head waiter who interrupts anyone when a VIP table calls.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::02 Microcontrollers & Embedded Linux
notes.front: When is a real-time operating system (RTOS) worth it on a microcontroller unit (MCU), and what does it cost?
notes.back: When activities with different rates/priorities coexist (1 kHz motor loop, 100 Hz fusion, comms, logging). Costs: RAM per task stack; new bugs (priority inversion, races, deadlock).

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::02 Microcontrollers & Embedded Linux
notes.front: What is a watchdog timer, and why should a mobile robot enable it?
notes.back: A hardware countdown that resets the microcontroller unit (MCU) unless firmware periodically 'kicks' it; if code hangs, the robot reboots into a safe state instead of driving on stale commands.
notes.analogy: A dead man's switch: let go (stop kicking) and the train stops.
notes.extra: Complement: a command timeout: stop motors if no fresh command arrives within ~200 ms.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::02 Microcontrollers & Embedded Linux
notes.front: What breaks if firmware kicks the watchdog from a timer interrupt instead of the main loop?
notes.back: The interrupt keeps feeding the watchdog even when the main loop hangs, so the reset never happens. Kick it only after the main loop has verified that its tasks ran.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::03 Sensors
notes.front: Proprioceptive vs. exteroceptive sensors?
notes.back:
Proprioceptive: robot's internal state (encoders, inertial measurement unit (IMU), motor current, joint torque).
Exteroceptive: the environment (camera, light detection and ranging (LiDAR), ultrasonic, tactile, global navigation satellite system (GNSS)).
notes.source: Siegwart, Nourbakhsh & Scaramuzza, Introduction to Autonomous Mobile Robots (2nd ed.)

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::03 Sensors
notes.front: Inertial measurement unit (IMU): what do '6-axis' and '9-axis' mean?
notes.back: 6-axis = 3-axis accelerometer (specific force) + 3-axis gyroscope (angular velocity). 9-axis adds a 3-axis magnetometer (heading).
notes.extra: Examples: MPU-6050 (6-axis); BNO055 (9-axis with on-chip fusion).
notes.source: Siegwart, Nourbakhsh & Scaramuzza, Introduction to Autonomous Mobile Robots (2nd ed.)

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::03 Sensors
notes.front: From an inertial measurement unit (IMU), which orientation angles are observable from gravity, and which isn't?
notes.back: Roll and pitch are observable from gravity; yaw needs a magnetometer or another absolute reference.
notes.source: Siegwart, Nourbakhsh & Scaramuzza, Introduction to Autonomous Mobile Robots (2nd ed.)

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::03 Sensors
notes.front: Why fuse gyroscope and accelerometer data?
notes.back: Gyro: smooth and fast but its integral drifts. Accelerometer: drift-free gravity direction but noisy and corrupted by motion. Each covers the other's weakness.
notes.analogy: Gyro is a stopwatch that slowly runs fast; the accelerometer is a jittery wall clock that's right on average. Trust the stopwatch short-term, the clock long-term.
notes.source: Siegwart, Nourbakhsh & Scaramuzza, Introduction to Autonomous Mobile Robots (2nd ed.)

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::03 Sensors
notes.front: Complementary filter for tilt: formula and interpretation?
notes.back: θ = α·(θ + ω·dt) + (1 − α)·θaccel, α ≈ 0.95–0.98: high-pass the gyro, low-pass the accelerometer.
notes.extra: Cheap alternative to a Kalman filter; Madgwick/Mahony extend it to 3D with quaternions.
notes.source: Siegwart, Nourbakhsh & Scaramuzza, Introduction to Autonomous Mobile Robots (2nd ed.)

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::03 Sensors
notes.front: In a complementary filter, what goes wrong if α is too close to 1, and if it is too small?
notes.back:
Too close to 1: the gyro dominates and drift is corrected very slowly.
Too small: the accelerometer dominates, so noise and motion-induced errors leak into the angle.
notes.source: Siegwart, Nourbakhsh & Scaramuzza, Introduction to Autonomous Mobile Robots (2nd ed.)

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::03 Sensors
notes.front: How does a quadrature encoder give both position and direction?
notes.back: Two channels A and B, 90° out of phase: which leads gives direction, counting edges gives displacement. Counting all edges of both = 4× pulses per revolution (PPR).
notes.extra: An optional index (Z) channel marks one absolute position per turn.
notes.source: Siegwart, Nourbakhsh & Scaramuzza, Introduction to Autonomous Mobile Robots (2nd ed.)

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::03 Sensors
notes.front: Why does an incremental encoder need two channels instead of one?
notes.back: One channel only counts pulses and cannot distinguish forward from backward. The second channel, 90° out of phase, shows which edge comes first, hence the direction.
notes.source: Siegwart, Nourbakhsh & Scaramuzza, Introduction to Autonomous Mobile Robots (2nd ed.)

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::03 Sensors
notes.front: Incremental vs. absolute encoders: practical difference for a robot arm?
notes.back:
Incremental: counts change only → position lost at power-off → needs homing.
Absolute (e.g. magnetic AS5600): true angle at power-on, no homing.
notes.extra: Absolute encoders are often placed on the joint output to see through gearbox backlash.
notes.source: Siegwart, Nourbakhsh & Scaramuzza, Introduction to Autonomous Mobile Robots (2nd ed.)

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::03 Sensors
notes.front: Output-shaft resolution: 12 pulses per revolution (PPR) motor encoder, quadrature decoding, 50:1 gearbox?
notes.back: 12 × 4 × 50 = 2400 counts/rev → 0.15° per count.
notes.extra: Wheel: distance per count = π·D / 2400.
notes.source: Siegwart, Nourbakhsh & Scaramuzza, Introduction to Autonomous Mobile Robots (2nd ed.)

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::03 Sensors
notes.front: How does an HC-SR04 ultrasonic sensor measure distance?
notes.back: 10 µs trigger → 40 kHz burst → echo pin HIGH for the round-trip time t; d = t × 343 m/s ÷ 2. Range ~2 cm–4 m.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::03 Sensors
notes.front: Limitations of ultrasonic range sensors?
notes.back: Wide cone (~15–30°), soft or angled surfaces reflect poorly, cross-talk between sensors, slow update, temperature-dependent speed of sound.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::03 Sensors
notes.front: Light detection and ranging (LiDAR) on robots: principle and main types?
notes.back: Laser time-of-flight. 2D spinning (RPLIDAR): indoor mapping/navigation standard. 3D multi-beam/solid-state: outdoor point clouds. Single-point ToF chips (VL53L1X): cheap short range.
notes.extra: Weak on: glass, mirrors, very dark surfaces.
notes.source: Siegwart, Nourbakhsh & Scaramuzza, Introduction to Autonomous Mobile Robots (2nd ed.)

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::03 Sensors
notes.text: Depth cameras: {{c1::stereo}} triangulates between two cameras (works outdoors, struggles on texture-less surfaces); {{c2::structured light}} projects a known pattern (accurate close up, fails in sunlight); {{c3::time-of-flight}} times light per pixel (good range, multipath issues).
notes.extra: Example: Intel RealSense D4xx = active stereo (infrared (IR) projector adds texture). All output red, green, blue (RGB)-D → point clouds.
notes.source: Siegwart, Nourbakhsh & Scaramuzza, Introduction to Autonomous Mobile Robots (2nd ed.)

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::03 Sensors
notes.front: What does a 6-axis force/torque sensor measure, and where is it mounted?
notes.back: Three forces and three torques (strain gauges), typically at the wrist between arm and gripper.
notes.extra: Uses: contact detection, force-controlled insertion, polishing, hand-guiding, collision safety, policy input.
notes.source: Siegwart, Nourbakhsh & Scaramuzza, Introduction to Autonomous Mobile Robots (2nd ed.)

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::03 Sensors
notes.front: Hall-effect sensor: what does it measure, and where does it appear in robots?
notes.back: Magnetic field (analog voltage or threshold switch). Uses: brushless direct current (BLDC) commutation, magnetic absolute encoders (AS5600), wheel-speed pickups, contactless limit switches, current sensing.
notes.source: Horowitz & Hill, The Art of Electronics (3rd ed.)

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::03 Sensors
notes.front: Sensor accuracy vs. precision vs. resolution?
notes.back: Accuracy: mean close to truth (bias). Precision: spread of repeated readings (noise). Resolution: smallest reportable change.
notes.analogy: Darts: accurate = centred on the bullseye; precise = tightly grouped; resolution = how finely the board is marked.
notes.extra: High resolution implies neither. Calibration fixes bias; averaging improves precision.
notes.source: Siegwart, Nourbakhsh & Scaramuzza, Introduction to Autonomous Mobile Robots (2nd ed.)

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::03 Sensors
notes.front: Vision-based tactile sensors (GelSight, DIGIT): how do they work?
notes.back: A camera watches the back of a soft, lit elastomer skin; contact deforms the gel and the image encodes contact geometry, shear/slip and force at high resolution.
notes.source: Kawaharazuka et al. 2025, VLA Models for Robotics: A Review

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::03 Sensors
notes.front: Why do vision-based tactile sensors suit manipulation learning?
notes.back: Their output is an image, so it plugs straight into vision encoders; several vision-language-action models (VLAs) add tactile tokens for contact-rich tasks like insertion.
notes.source: Kawaharazuka et al. 2025, VLA Models for Robotics: A Review

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::04 Actuators & Power Transmission
notes.front: Brushed direct current (DC) motor: what sets speed and what sets torque?
notes.back: Speed ∝ voltage (minus back-EMF); torque ∝ current (τ = Kt·I).
notes.extra: Consequences: control speed with pulse-width modulation (PWM) duty; motor current is a cheap torque estimate; stall = max current.
notes.source: Hughes & Drury, Electric Motors and Drives (5th ed.)

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::04 Actuators & Power Transmission
notes.front: A brushed direct current (DC) motor is stalled. What current flows, and what does it mean for driver sizing?
notes.back: No back electromotive force (back-EMF) at stall, so I = V/R, the maximum. Size the driver, supply and thermal protection for stall current, not running current.
notes.source: Hughes & Drury, Electric Motors and Drives (5th ed.)

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::04 Actuators & Power Transmission
notes.front: What is an H-bridge, and how does it control a direct current (DC) motor?
notes.back: Four switches around the motor: closing diagonal pairs reverses polarity (forward/reverse); pulse-width modulation (PWM) on enable sets speed; both low sides on = brake.
notes.analogy: Like an H-shaped set of railway points: flip the diagonal pair and the train runs through the motor the other way.
notes.extra: Never close both switches on one side: shoot-through short.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::04 Actuators & Power Transmission
notes.front: What is shoot-through in an H-bridge, and how is it prevented?
notes.back: Both switches of one half-bridge on at once short the supply to ground through them. Prevent with dead time between switching, or a driver chip that enforces it.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::04 Actuators & Power Transmission
notes.front: Why move from the L298N to metal-oxide-semiconductor field-effect transistor (MOSFET) motor drivers (TB6612FNG, DRV8833)?
notes.back: The L298N's bipolar transistors drop ~2 V (hot, inefficient); MOSFET drivers drop a fraction of a volt.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::04 Actuators & Power Transmission
notes.front: Hobby servo: what is the control signal?
notes.back: 50 Hz pulses (20 ms period); width 1.0–2.0 ms ≈ 0–180°, 1.5 ms = centre (many accept 0.5–2.5 ms).

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::04 Actuators & Power Transmission
notes.front: What is inside a hobby servo, and how should it be powered?
notes.back: Direct current (DC) motor + gearbox + potentiometer + closed-loop position controller (no feedback to you). Power from a separate 5–6 V rail; stall can exceed 1 A.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::04 Actuators & Power Transmission
notes.front: How does a stepper motor move, and how is it driven?
notes.back: Coils energised in sequence move the rotor in fixed steps (typically 1.8° = 200 steps/rev; microstepping smooths it). Drivers (A4988, TMC2209) chop coil current; control via STEP/DIR.
notes.source: Hughes & Drury, Electric Motors and Drives (5th ed.)

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::04 Actuators & Power Transmission
notes.front: Why choose a stepper motor for positioning without a position sensor?
notes.back: Each step is a fixed angle, so position follows from counting step pulses (open-loop), and it has strong holding torque at standstill.
notes.source: Hughes & Drury, Electric Motors and Drives (5th ed.)

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::04 Actuators & Power Transmission
notes.front: Stepper motor: what are its main weaknesses?
notes.back: Torque falls with speed; draws full current at standstill; resonance; and lost steps go undetected without feedback.
notes.source: Hughes & Drury, Electric Motors and Drives (5th ed.)

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::04 Actuators & Power Transmission
notes.front: A stepper driven open-loop is overloaded for a moment. What happens, and how do you detect it?
notes.back: It skips steps: the controller's position count silently no longer matches reality. Detect with an encoder or homing switch, or use a closed-loop stepper.
notes.source: Hughes & Drury, Electric Motors and Drives (5th ed.)

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::04 Actuators & Power Transmission
notes.front: Brushless direct current (BLDC) vs. brushed motor: how is a BLDC commutated?
notes.back: Electronically: a controller switches the three-phase stator using Hall sensors, an encoder or sensorless back-EMF.
notes.extra: Standard in drones, quadrupeds, humanoids and modern arms.
notes.source: Hughes & Drury, Electric Motors and Drives (5th ed.)

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::04 Actuators & Power Transmission
notes.front: Brushless direct current (BLDC) motor: pros and cons vs. brushed?
notes.back:
+ Higher efficiency and power density, long life, less electrical noise.
− Needs a three-phase inverter/controller (electronic speed controller (ESC) or field-oriented control (FOC) drive).
notes.source: Hughes & Drury, Electric Motors and Drives (5th ed.)

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::04 Actuators & Power Transmission
notes.front: Which motor suits a drone propeller, and which a 3D-printer axis, and why?
notes.back:
Drone propeller: brushless direct current (BLDC), for efficiency and power density.
3D-printer axis: stepper, for precise open-loop positioning without a sensor.
notes.source: Hughes & Drury, Electric Motors and Drives (5th ed.)

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::04 Actuators & Power Transmission
notes.front: Field-Oriented Control (FOC): what is the core trick?
notes.back: Transform phase currents into the rotor-aligned d/q frame (Clarke + Park), where they are direct current (DC) quantities, so simple proportional-integral (PI) loops regulate Iq (torque) and hold Id ≈ 0.
notes.analogy: Like describing a merry-go-round rider from a seat on the ride: in the rotating frame they're standing still, so control is easy.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::04 Actuators & Power Transmission
notes.front: Why is field-oriented control (FOC) the basis of torque-controlled robot joints?
notes.back: Smooth, quiet, efficient torque control down to zero speed (ODrive, SimpleFOC, moteus).

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::04 Actuators & Power Transmission
notes.front: Gearbox N:1: how do output speed, torque and reflected rotor inertia change?
notes.back: Speed ÷ N; torque × N (× efficiency); reflected inertia × N².

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::04 Actuators & Power Transmission
notes.front: A motor delivers 0.1 N·m. With a 50:1 gearbox at 80% efficiency, what are the output torque and speed change?
notes.back: Torque = 0.1 × 50 × 0.8 = 4 N·m; output speed is 1/50 of the motor speed.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::04 Actuators & Power Transmission
notes.front: Downside of high gear ratios in robot joints?
notes.back: Slow joints that are hard to back-drive, with external forces hidden behind friction and reflected inertia (N²).
notes.analogy: A bike in its lowest gear climbs anything, but you can't feel the road and can't pedal fast.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::04 Actuators & Power Transmission
notes.front: On a direct current (DC) motor's torque–speed line, where is mechanical power maximal?
notes.back: At half no-load speed and half stall torque (P = τ·ω on a linear line).
notes.extra: Pick motor + gear ratio so the operating point sits near here, not near stall (overheating).
notes.source: Hughes & Drury, Electric Motors and Drives (5th ed.)

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::04 Actuators & Power Transmission
notes.front: What is back-EMF, and how does it shape motor current?
notes.back: A spinning motor is a generator: V<sub>emf</sub> = K<sub>e</sub>·ω opposes the supply, so I = (V − K<sub>e</sub>ω)/R: highest at stall, falling with speed.
notes.extra: Uses: sensorless speed estimation/commutation. Hazard: a driven or braking motor pumps energy back into the supply.
notes.source: Hughes & Drury, Electric Motors and Drives (5th ed.)

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::04 Actuators & Power Transmission
notes.front: What is a Quasi-Direct-Drive (QDD) actuator?
notes.back: A high-torque-density 'pancake' brushless direct current (BLDC) with a low gear ratio (~6–10:1) and no torque sensor; torque is estimated from motor current.
notes.source: Wensing et al. 2017, Proprioceptive Actuator Design in the MIT Cheetah (IEEE T-RO)

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::04 Actuators & Power Transmission
notes.front: Why did quasi-direct drive (QDD) actuators transform legged robots?
notes.back: Low reflected inertia and friction make them back-drivable and impact-tolerant, with accurate current-based torque control; easy to simulate, so reinforcement learning (RL) policies transfer.
notes.analogy: A QDD leg is like a human leg with relaxed muscles: it gives on impact and you feel the ground through it.
notes.extra: Pioneered in MIT Cheetah; now standard in Unitree quadrupeds and many humanoids.
notes.source: Wensing et al. 2017, Proprioceptive Actuator Design in the MIT Cheetah (IEEE T-RO)

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::04 Actuators & Power Transmission
notes.front: What is a Series Elastic Actuator (SEA)?
notes.back: A deliberate spring between gearbox and load; measuring its deflection gives torque (Hooke's law), turning force control into position control.
notes.extra: Used in: Baxter, NASA Valkyrie, ANYmal.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::04 Actuators & Power Transmission
notes.front: Series elastic actuator (SEA) trade-off?
notes.back:
+ Accurate force control, shock tolerance, energy storage.
− Lower control bandwidth.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::04 Actuators & Power Transmission
notes.front: Planetary vs. strain-wave vs. cycloidal reducers: one-line niche each?
notes.back:
Planetary: cheap, back-drivable at low ratios, some backlash (quasi-direct drive (QDD) legs).
Strain-wave: 50–160:1, near-zero backlash, poor back-drive (industrial/cobot arms).
Cycloidal: high ratio, shock-robust, heavier.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::04 Actuators & Power Transmission
notes.front: What is a smart bus servo (Dynamixel, Feetech STS3215)?
notes.back: A servo with its own microcontroller unit (MCU) on a daisy-chained serial bus; each has an ID and reports position, velocity, load, voltage and temperature.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::04 Actuators & Power Transmission
notes.front: Why do low-cost learning arms (SO-101) use bus servos?
notes.back: Readable joint states on both the hand-moved leader and the follower arm with minimal wiring: exactly what imitation learning needs.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::05 Communication Protocols
notes.front: Universal asynchronous receiver-transmitter (UART): how does it work?
notes.back: Asynchronous point-to-point serial: transmit (TX)→receive (RX) crossed plus common ground; no clock line, so both ends must agree on the baud rate.
notes.analogy: Two people tapping Morse code with no shared metronome: it only works if both agreed the tempo beforehand.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::05 Communication Protocols
notes.front: Two universal asynchronous receiver-transmitters (UARTs) show garbage characters. What is the most likely cause?
notes.back: A mismatched baud rate or frame format. With no clock line, the receiver samples at the wrong moments. Check baud, data bits, parity and stop bits on both ends.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::05 Communication Protocols
notes.front: Universal asynchronous receiver-transmitter (UART): what does '115200 8N1' mean?
notes.back: 115 200 bit/s, 8 data bits, No parity, 1 stop bit; with the start bit that's 10 bits on the wire per byte.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::05 Communication Protocols
notes.front: Inter-integrated circuit (I2C): wiring and addressing?
notes.back: Two open-drain lines, serial data (SDA) and serial clock (SCL), with pull-up resistors (~2.2–10 kΩ); one controller, many targets selected by 7-bit address.
notes.extra: Speeds: 100 kbit/s standard, 400 kbit/s fast, 1 Mbit/s fast-mode plus.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::05 Communication Protocols
notes.front: Why are inter-integrated circuit (I2C) lines open-drain with pull-ups instead of push-pull?
notes.back: Devices can only pull a line low or release it, so one device driving low and another "high" can never short the bus. This makes sharing the wires safe.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::05 Communication Protocols
notes.front: Two identical sensors with the same fixed inter-integrated circuit (I2C) address share one bus. What happens, and what are the fixes?
notes.back: Both answer the same address, so reads collide or return garbage. Fix: address-select pins, a multiplexer (TCA9548A), or a second bus.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::05 Communication Protocols
notes.front: Why do inter-integrated circuit (I2C) buses need pull-up resistors, and why does long wiring break them?
notes.back: Lines are open-drain: devices only pull low, so resistors must pull them high. Wire capacitance slows the rising edge (RC time constant), so long wires need stronger pull-ups, shorter runs or a lower speed.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::05 Communication Protocols
notes.front: An inter-integrated circuit (I2C) bus hangs with serial data (SDA) held low. What happened, and how do you recover?
notes.back: A target was mid-transfer when the controller reset and still holds SDA low (bus lock-up). Recover by clocking the serial clock (SCL) up to 9 times, or power-cycle the target.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::05 Communication Protocols
notes.front: Serial peripheral interface (SPI): wiring and characteristics?
notes.back: Serial clock (SCK), master out, slave in (MOSI)/COPI, master in, slave out (MISO)/CIPO and one chip-select per device; full-duplex, push-pull, no addressing, tens of Mbit/s. Clock mode (0–3) must match.
notes.extra: Used for: displays, secure digital (SD) cards, high-rate inertial measurement units (IMUs), external analog-to-digital converters (ADCs), encoder chips.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::05 Communication Protocols
notes.front: Universal asynchronous receiver-transmitter (UART) vs. inter-integrated circuit (I2C) vs. serial peripheral interface (SPI): when to pick each?
notes.back:
UART: two devices, simple streams (GPS, board-to-board).
I2C: many slow sensors on two wires.
SPI: high rate/low latency, few devices.
notes.extra: None is robust over long noisy cables; use differential buses (controller area network (CAN), RS-485).

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::05 Communication Protocols
notes.front: Controller area network (CAN) bus: physical layer and topology?
notes.back: Two-wire differential bus (CAN_H/CAN_L), multi-master, 120 Ω termination at each end.
notes.source: Bosch CAN 2.0 spec / CAN in Automation

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::05 Communication Protocols
notes.front: Why does a controller area network (CAN) bus need 120 Ω termination at both ends?
notes.back: It matches the cable's characteristic impedance so signals are not reflected at the ends; reflections would corrupt bits at higher speeds.
notes.source: Bosch CAN 2.0 spec / CAN in Automation

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::05 Communication Protocols
notes.front: Controller area network (CAN) arbitration: how is priority decided?
notes.back: Messages carry an identifier, not an address; bitwise arbitration where dominant 0 beats recessive 1, so the lowest ID wins, non-destructively.
notes.analogy: Everyone starts speaking at once, but whoever says '0' first keeps talking and the others politely fall silent; no one's sentence is garbled.
notes.extra: Built-in cyclic redundancy check (CRC), acknowledgement (ACK) and automatic retransmission. Classical CAN: ≤1 Mbit/s, 8 data bytes.
notes.source: Bosch CAN 2.0 spec / CAN in Automation

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::05 Communication Protocols
notes.front: What does controller area network (CAN) flexible data-rate (FD) add over classical CAN?
notes.back: Up to 64 data bytes per frame and a faster data phase (typically 2–8 Mbit/s).
notes.source: Bosch CAN 2.0 spec / CAN in Automation

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::05 Communication Protocols
notes.front: Why is controller area network (CAN) the default bus for robot joint actuators?
notes.back: Noise immunity near motors, just two wires daisy-chained through limbs, deterministic priority, built-in error handling, cheap transceivers.
notes.extra: Used by: ODrive, moteus, Mini-Cheetah-style actuators, many humanoids.
notes.source: Bosch CAN 2.0 spec / CAN in Automation

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::05 Communication Protocols
notes.front: RS-485: what is it, and how does it differ from controller area network (CAN)?
notes.back: A differential electrical standard (not a protocol): multi-drop, long cables (~1200 m), usually half-duplex. Unlike CAN it has no arbitration or error handling; the protocol on top must add them.
notes.extra: Carries: Modbus remote terminal unit (RTU), Dynamixel Protocol 2.0, Digital Multiplex (DMX).
notes.source: Horowitz & Hill, The Art of Electronics (3rd ed.)

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::05 Communication Protocols
notes.front: EtherCAT: how does it achieve very short cycle times?
notes.back: One Ethernet frame passes through every device in a line/ring; each reads and writes its data on the fly in hardware. Distributed clocks sync nodes to <1 µs.
notes.analogy: A train that never stops: each station grabs and drops parcels from the moving carriages as it passes.
notes.extra: → 1 ms down to ~100 µs cycles with dozens of axes (high-end arms, humanoids).

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::05 Communication Protocols
notes.front: Why never close a fast control loop over Wi-Fi?
notes.back: Wi-Fi/Bluetooth latency is variable (ms to s) with packet loss; that delay inside a feedback loop causes instability.
notes.source: Siegwart, Nourbakhsh & Scaramuzza, Introduction to Autonomous Mobile Robots (2nd ed.)

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::05 Communication Protocols
notes.front: How is wireless used properly on robots?
notes.back: Stabilising loops run on board; wireless carries only set-points, tele-op commands and telemetry, with a command timeout/fail-safe and best-effort (User Datagram Protocol (UDP)-style) streams for fresh data.
notes.source: Siegwart, Nourbakhsh & Scaramuzza, Introduction to Autonomous Mobile Robots (2nd ed.)

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::05 Communication Protocols
notes.front: Custom Pi↔microcontroller unit (MCU) serial protocol: what must every packet have?
notes.back:
• Framing (start byte + length, or Consistent Overhead Byte Stuffing (COBS) with 0x00 delimiter) to resynchronise
  • Integrity check (checksum/CRC)
  • Message type + fixed binary layout (endianness, padding)
notes.extra: Also: timeouts and sequence numbers. Or reuse micro-ROS, MAVLink, nanopb.
notes.source: Horowitz & Hill, The Art of Electronics (3rd ed.)

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::05 Communication Protocols
notes.front: What is MAVLink?
notes.back: A lightweight binary messaging protocol between drones/rovers, companion computers and ground stations (HEARTBEAT, ATTITUDE, missions); used by PX4 and ArduPilot.
notes.extra: Robot Operating System (ROS) 2 bridges: MAVROS; PX4's native uXRCE-DDS bridge.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::02 Microcontrollers & Embedded Linux
notes.front: Raspberry Pi general-purpose input/output (GPIO) electrical rules?
notes.back: 3.3 V, NOT 5 V tolerant; ~16 mA per pin, ~50 mA total; no analog inputs (add an MCP3008/ADS1115 analog-to-digital converter (ADC)).
notes.extra: Header also offers inter-integrated circuit (I2C), serial peripheral interface (SPI), universal asynchronous receiver-transmitter (UART), two hardware pulse-width modulation (PWM) channels, 5 V and 3.3 V rails.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::02 Microcontrollers & Embedded Linux
notes.front: Register-poking general-purpose input/output (GPIO) code breaks on a new single-board computer (SBC) revision. Why, and what should you use instead?
notes.back: The GPIO block moved (on the Raspberry Pi 5 to the separate RP1 chip), so libraries that write hardware registers directly (RPi.GPIO, pigpio) break. Use the kernel GPIO character device via libgpiod (or wrappers such as lgpio, gpiozero), which is stable across boards.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::02 Microcontrollers & Embedded Linux
notes.front: Why does software pulse-width modulation (PWM) from Linux make servos jitter, and what fixes it?
notes.back: The scheduler pre-empts user-space timing, so pulse widths wobble by 10s–100s of µs. Fix: hardware PWM channels, a PCA9685 inter-integrated circuit (I2C) PWM chip, or a microcontroller unit (MCU).

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::02 Microcontrollers & Embedded Linux
notes.front: What does PREEMPT_RT give Linux?
notes.back: Nearly all kernel code becomes pre-emptible and interrupt request (IRQ) handlers become threads → bounded worst-case latency (tens to ~100 µs) for SCHED_FIFO threads; enough for ~1 kHz loops.
notes.analogy: It doesn't make the car faster; it guarantees the ambulance always gets through the traffic within a fixed time.
notes.extra: Merged into mainline in kernel 6.12 (2024). Used for ros2_control, EtherCAT masters.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::02 Microcontrollers & Embedded Linux
notes.front: What does PREEMPT_RT not give you?
notes.back: Speed. You must still avoid page faults (mlockall), dynamic allocation and blocking I/O in the real-time path.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::02 Microcontrollers & Embedded Linux
notes.front: Canonical two-tier compute architecture of a mobile robot?
notes.back:
Linux computer (Pi/Jetson): cameras, light detection and ranging (LiDAR), simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM), planning, Robot Operating System (ROS) 2, AI.
Microcontroller: encoders, proportional-integral-derivative (PID) loops at 100 Hz–1 kHz+, inertial measurement unit (IMU), safety timeouts.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::02 Microcontrollers & Embedded Linux
notes.front: Two-tier robot: what crosses the Linux↔microcontroller unit (MCU) interface?
notes.back: Velocity commands down (e.g. cmd_vel), odometry and sensor data up, over USB/UART, controller area network (CAN) or micro-ROS.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::02 Microcontrollers & Embedded Linux
notes.front: Two camera stacks on an embedded Linux board: how does each reach OpenCV?
notes.back: Camera serial interface (CSI) ribbon cameras go through libcamera (on Raspberry Pi: rpicam-apps and the Picamera2 library); USB webcams appear as Video4Linux2 (V4L2) devices that OpenCV's VideoCapture opens directly.
notes.extra: Board-specific legacy camera APIs (raspistill/picamera) are gone; old tutorials mislead.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::02 Microcontrollers & Embedded Linux
notes.front: Edge neural processing unit (NPU) accelerator vs GPU: what can and can't a few-watt NPU (e.g. Hailo on a Pi hardware attached on top (HAT)) do?
notes.back: It runs compiled vision nets (detection, segmentation, pose) in real time at a few watts. It is not a general GPU: no CUDA, limited operator support, and it won't run large vision-language-action models (VLAs) or arbitrary PyTorch models.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::02 Microcontrollers & Embedded Linux
notes.front: When does a robot need an on-board GPU computer (e.g. NVIDIA Jetson) instead of a plain single-board computer (SBC)?
notes.back: When you need an on-board GPU: deep-learning perception, GPU-accelerated simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM), or running learned policies on the robot.
notes.extra: Trade-offs: higher cost, power and cooling; size the module by the tera operations per second (TOPS) and memory your models need, not by the top of the vendor's range.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::02 Microcontrollers & Embedded Linux
notes.front: Pi robot under-voltage: symptoms, check and fix?
notes.back: Throttling, random reboots, USB drop-outs when motors start. Check vcgencmd get_throttled (non-zero = trouble). Fix: dedicated 5 V/5 A buck, short thick leads.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::02 Microcontrollers & Embedded Linux
notes.front: How do you protect a Pi robot from secure digital (SD)-card corruption?
notes.back: Provide a clean-shutdown path, use a read-only/overlay root filesystem or boot from non-volatile memory express (NVMe)/SSD, and log to RAM or external storage.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::02 Microcontrollers & Embedded Linux
notes.front: Minimal OpenCV colour-tracking pipeline to steer toward a ball?
notes.back: Frame → hue, saturation, value (HSV) → inRange() mask (+erode/dilate) → largest contour → centroid. Steering error = centroid x − image centre; contour area ≈ distance.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::02 Microcontrollers & Embedded Linux
notes.front: Why convert to hue, saturation, value (HSV) for colour tracking?
notes.back: Hue separates colour from brightness, so thresholds are more robust to lighting than in blue, green, red (BGR).

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::02 Microcontrollers & Embedded Linux
notes.front: What is special about the RP2040/RP2350's programmable input/output (PIO)?
notes.back: Programmable I/O state machines implement custom, cycle-exact protocols in hardware: quadrature decoding, WS2812 light-emitting diodes (LEDs), extra universal asynchronous receiver-transmitters (UARTs).

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::02 Microcontrollers & Embedded Linux
notes.front: Simplest way to run Robot Operating System (ROS) 2 on a Raspberry Pi?
notes.back: Install 64-bit Ubuntu (ROS 2 Tier-1 platform) and apt install the matching distro. On Raspberry Pi OS: Docker or build from source.
notes.extra: Tip: run RViz on a laptop in the same ROS domain; keep only drivers and navigation on the Pi.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::06 Control Theory
notes.front: Open-loop vs. closed-loop control?
notes.back:
Open-loop: command without measuring the result; simple but blind to disturbances.
Closed-loop: measure, compute error e = r − y, correct; rejects disturbances but can go unstable if badly tuned.
notes.analogy: Open-loop is driving with your eyes shut after memorising the route; closed-loop is driving while watching the road.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::06 Control Theory
notes.front: Proportional-integral-derivative (PID) control law?
notes.back: u = K<sub>p</sub>·e + K<sub>i</sub>·∫e dt + K<sub>d</sub>·de/dt

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::06 Control Theory
notes.text: Proportional-integral-derivative (PID) terms: P reacts to the {{c1::present error}} (more gain = faster, but {{c2::more overshoot}}); I {{c3::accumulates past error}} to remove steady-state error; D reacts to the error's {{c4::rate of change}}, adding damping but amplifying {{c5::noise}}.
notes.analogy: Steering a boat: P turns toward the line, I corrects for a steady current, D eases off as you approach so you don't overshoot.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::06 Control Theory
notes.front: Which proportional-integral-derivative (PID) term removes a constant offset, which reduces overshoot, and what does each cost?
notes.back:
Integral: removes the offset but risks windup and slower, oscillatory response.
Derivative: damps overshoot but amplifies sensor noise.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::06 Control Theory
notes.front: Why does a P-only velocity loop never quite reach the set-point, and what fixes it?
notes.back: Holding speed against friction needs a non-zero command, which P-only can only produce from a non-zero error. Fix: integral action and/or feedforward.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::06 Control Theory
notes.front: Practical fixes that make the proportional-integral-derivative (PID) derivative term usable on real hardware?
notes.back: Low-pass filter it (noise); derivative on measurement (−Kd·dy/dt) to avoid 'derivative kick' on set-point steps; accurate, consistent dt.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::06 Control Theory
notes.front: What is integral windup?
notes.back: While the actuator is saturated, the integrator keeps accumulating error it can't act on; when the error reverses, the stored integral causes big overshoot.
notes.analogy: Pushing harder on a door that's already wide open: when it finally swings back, all that pent-up push sends you flying.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::06 Control Theory
notes.front: A proportional-integral-derivative (PID)-controlled arm is held back by hand while the controller pushes, then released and lurches past the target. Why?
notes.back: Integral windup: the integrator kept accumulating while the actuator was saturated, and the stored value now drives a big overshoot. Fix with anti-windup.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::06 Control Theory
notes.front: Anti-windup methods?
notes.back: Clamp the integrator; stop integrating while saturated (conditional integration); back-calculation (bleed by the saturation excess).

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::06 Control Theory
notes.front: What does a discrete proportional-integral-derivative (PID) on a microcontroller unit (MCU) need that the textbook formula hides?
notes.back: A fixed, known sample period (timer interrupt or scheduled task); integral ≈ Σe·dt, derivative ≈ Δ/dt. Timing jitter acts like noise on D.
notes.extra: Also: output clamping + anti-windup, derivative filtering, no blocking calls in the loop.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::06 Control Theory
notes.front: Ziegler–Nichols ultimate-gain tuning: procedure?
notes.back: With I = D = 0, raise Kp until sustained oscillation → Ku and period Tu. Classic proportional-integral-derivative (PID): Kp = 0.6Ku, Ti = Tu/2, Td = Tu/8.
notes.extra: Aggressive (~quarter-decay) starting point, not a final tune. Don't drive fragile mechanisms to oscillation.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::06 Control Theory
notes.text: Step-response metrics: {{c1::rise time}} (10→90%), {{c2::overshoot}} (peak excess, %), {{c3::settling time}} (stays within ±2%), {{c4::steady-state error}} (remaining offset).
notes.extra: Second-order system: overshoot set by damping ratio ζ, speed by natural frequency ω<sub>n</sub>.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::06 Control Theory
notes.front: What is cascaded control in a servo drive?
notes.back: Nested loops: position → velocity → current. Each loop commands the set-point of the one inside it.
notes.analogy: A manager sets goals for a team lead, who sets tasks for a worker: each level reacts at its own speed.
notes.extra: Benefits: disturbances rejected near where they enter; current/speed limits enforced naturally; tune inside-out.
notes.source: Siciliano, Sciavicco, Villani & Oriolo, Robotics: Modelling, Planning and Control

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::06 Control Theory
notes.front: Cascaded control: rule for loop rates?
notes.back: Each inner loop ~5–10× faster than the one around it (e.g. current 10–20 kHz, velocity 1–5 kHz, position ~1 kHz).
notes.source: Siciliano, Sciavicco, Villani & Oriolo, Robotics: Modelling, Planning and Control

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::06 Control Theory
notes.front: Why must an inner control loop run faster than the loop around it?
notes.back: So the outer loop sees the inner one as nearly instantaneous (time-scale separation). With similar rates the loops interact and can destabilise each other.
notes.source: Siciliano, Sciavicco, Villani & Oriolo, Robotics: Modelling, Planning and Control

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::06 Control Theory
notes.front: What is feedforward control, and why combine it with feedback?
notes.back: A model-based command added to the feedback output (kv·v, ka·a, gravity g(q)). It acts before error appears and doesn't affect stability, so feedback only handles model error → better tracking with lower gains.
notes.analogy: Leaning into a turn before the bike starts to tip, rather than waiting to correct the wobble.
notes.extra: Classic example: gravity compensation on an arm.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::06 Control Theory
notes.front: How fast must a digital control loop sample?
notes.back: Rule of thumb: 10–20× the desired closed-loop bandwidth (Nyquist's 2× only avoids aliasing), with an anti-aliasing filter before the analog-to-digital converter (ADC).
notes.extra: Latency matters as much as rate: computation + communication delay eats phase margin.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::06 Control Theory
notes.front: State-space model and stability condition (continuous and discrete)?
notes.back: ẋ = Ax + Bu, y = Cx + Du. Stable ⇔ eigenvalues of A have negative real part; discrete: eigenvalues inside the unit circle.
notes.extra: Non-linear robots are linearised around an operating point (e.g. upright pendulum).

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::06 Control Theory
notes.front: Controllability vs. observability?
notes.back:
Controllable: inputs can drive the state anywhere (→ arbitrary pole placement).
Observable: state can be reconstructed from outputs (→ observer/Kalman filter possible).
notes.extra: Example: yaw is unobservable from an accelerometer alone.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::06 Control Theory
notes.front: Rank test for controllability of ẋ = Ax + Bu with n states?
notes.back: rank [B AB … A<sup>n−1</sup>B] = n

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::06 Control Theory
notes.front: Rank test for observability of y = Cx with n states?
notes.back: rank [C; CA; …; CA<sup>n−1</sup>] = n

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::06 Control Theory
notes.front: If the controllability matrix is rank-deficient, what does that mean physically?
notes.back: Some state directions cannot be influenced by any input, so no controller can move the state anywhere or place all poles.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::06 Control Theory
notes.front: What is LQR?
notes.back: Optimal linear state feedback u = −Kx minimising ∫(xᵀQx + uᵀRu)dt; K from the algebraic Riccati equation.
notes.extra: Workhorse for balancing robots, quadrotors and stabilising trajectories (time-varying linear-quadratic regulator (LQR)).

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::06 Control Theory
notes.front: Linear-quadratic regulator (LQR) tuning: what do Q and R trade off?
notes.back: Q penalises state error, R penalises actuator effort; tuning = choosing these weights. Good margins given full state.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::06 Control Theory
notes.front: What is Model Predictive Control (MPC)?
notes.back: Each step: solve a finite-horizon optimal-control problem from the current state subject to constraints, apply only the first input, shift and repeat (receding horizon).
notes.analogy: Chess: plan several moves ahead, play only the next one, then re-plan after seeing the reply.
notes.extra: + Handles constraints and preview. − Needs a model and real-time optimisation. Used in legged locomotion, driving, drones.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::06 Control Theory
notes.front: Gain margin and phase margin?
notes.back: Gain margin: factor loop gain can rise before instability (at −180° phase). Phase margin: extra lag tolerated (at unity gain). Targets ≥6 dB and 45–60°.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::06 Control Theory
notes.front: Why does latency destabilise a control loop?
notes.back: A time delay subtracts phase (−ω·Td), eating the phase margin.
notes.analogy: Steering with a laggy video feed: you keep correcting for where the car was, and start to weave.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::06 Control Theory
notes.front: Impedance/admittance control: what is regulated instead of pure position or force?
notes.back: The dynamic relationship between motion and contact force: the robot behaves like a virtual mass-spring-damper, F = K(xd − x) + D(ẋd − ẋ).
notes.analogy: Holding a cup with a firm but springy grip instead of a vice: you yield to bumps but still return to where you intended.
notes.source: Siciliano, Sciavicco, Villani & Oriolo, Robotics: Modelling, Planning and Control

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::06 Control Theory
notes.front: Impedance vs. admittance control: which needs what hardware?
notes.back:
Impedance: measure motion → command torque; needs torque-controllable, back-drivable joints.
Admittance: measure force → command motion; suits stiff position-controlled arms with a wrist F/T sensor.
notes.source: Siciliano, Sciavicco, Villani & Oriolo, Robotics: Modelling, Planning and Control

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::06 Control Theory
notes.front: Computed-torque (inverse-dynamics) control: what does it do?
notes.back: τ = M(q)(q̈d + Kdė + Kpe) + C(q,q̇)q̇ + g(q): the model cancels the non-linear coupled dynamics, leaving decoupled linear error dynamics per joint.
notes.extra: Needs a good model and torque-controlled joints; more accurate at speed than independent joint proportional-integral-derivative (PID).

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::06 Control Theory
notes.front: What is Whole-Body Control on a humanoid/legged robot?
notes.back: A ~1 kHz controller computing all joint torques at once by solving a constrained quadratic programming (QP) over the floating-base dynamics, with weighted/prioritised tasks (balance, feet, hands, posture).
notes.extra: Constraints: friction cones, torque and joint limits. Sits beneath model predictive control (MPC)/footstep planning; increasingly complemented by reinforcement learning (RL) whole-body policies.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::07 Kinematics & Dynamics
notes.front: Degrees of Freedom (DoF): definition, and for a free rigid body?
notes.back: Minimum number of independent coordinates specifying the configuration: 6 in space, 3 in the plane.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::07 Kinematics & Dynamics
notes.front: Grübler's formula?
notes.back: dof = m(N − 1 − J) + Σf<sub>i</sub>; m = 6 (spatial) or 3 (planar), N = links incl. ground, J = joints, f<sub>i</sub> = freedoms of joint i.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::07 Kinematics & Dynamics
notes.front: Why do most general-purpose robot arms have at least 6 joints?
notes.back: An arbitrary position (3) plus orientation (3) in space needs 6 independent degrees of freedom (DoF); fewer joints reach only a subset of poses.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::07 Kinematics & Dynamics
notes.text: {{c1::Configuration space}} = all joint configurations q (dimension = degrees of freedom (DoF)); {{c2::task space}} = where the task is expressed (e.g. end-effector pose); {{c3::workspace}} = poses the end-effector can reach (a robot property).

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::07 Kinematics & Dynamics
notes.front: What properties define a rotation matrix?
notes.back: R ∈ SO(3): RᵀR = I, det R = +1. Hence R⁻¹ = Rᵀ; columns = body axes in the reference frame; composition doesn't commute.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::07 Kinematics & Dynamics
notes.front: What is gimbal lock?
notes.back: A singularity of three-angle (Euler/RPY) representations: at a middle angle (pitch ±90°) the first and third axes align and a degrees of freedom (DoF) is lost. A flaw of the representation, not the rotation.
notes.analogy: Like longitude at the North Pole: every longitude meets there, so 'which way is east' stops meaning anything, though nothing is wrong with the Earth.
notes.extra: Avoid with rotation matrices or quaternions internally.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::07 Kinematics & Dynamics
notes.front: Why are unit quaternions the standard orientation representation in robot software?
notes.back: 4 numbers, no gimbal lock, cheap to compose and renormalise, smooth interpolation (SLERP).

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::07 Kinematics & Dynamics
notes.front: Quaternion pitfalls?
notes.back: Double cover (q and −q are the same rotation); and ordering conventions: Robot Operating System (ROS) uses (x, y, z, w), Eigen's constructor (w, x, y, z).

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::07 Kinematics & Dynamics
notes.front: Homogeneous transformation matrix: structure and key operations?
notes.back: 4×4 T = [[R, p], [0, 1]] ∈ SE(3). Maps points p<sub>a</sub> = T<sub>ab</sub>p<sub>b</sub>; chains T<sub>ac</sub> = T<sub>ab</sub>T<sub>bc</sub>; inverse [[Rᵀ, −Rᵀp], [0, 1]].
notes.extra: Backbone of forward kinematics, camera extrinsics and Robot Operating System (ROS) tf2.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::07 Kinematics & Dynamics
notes.front: Forward kinematics: what is it, and why is it easy for serial arms?
notes.back: Map joint values q to end-effector pose T(q) by chaining link transforms; for serial chains it's always unique (the opposite holds for parallel robots).

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::07 Kinematics & Dynamics
notes.front: Denavit–Hartenberg (DH) vs. Product of Exponentials (PoE) for forward kinematics?
notes.back:
DH: a frame per link by convention, T = A1…An.
PoE: T = e[S1]θ1…e[Sn]θnM with screw axes in the base frame; no per-link frames.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::07 Kinematics & Dynamics
notes.text: Denavit–Hartenberg (DH) parameters: a = {{c1::link length (along x)}}, α = {{c2::link twist (about x)}}, d = {{c3::link offset (along z)}}, θ = {{c4::joint angle (about z)}}.
notes.extra: Revolute: θ is variable; prismatic: d. 'Standard' and 'modified' (Craig) conventions differ.
notes.source: Siciliano, Sciavicco, Villani & Oriolo, Robotics: Modelling, Planning and Control

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::07 Kinematics & Dynamics
notes.front: What makes inverse kinematics hard?
notes.back: Non-linear, with zero, several (up to 8 for a 6R arm with spherical wrist) or infinitely many solutions.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::07 Kinematics & Dynamics
notes.front: Analytic vs. numerical inverse kinematics (IK)?
notes.back:
Analytic: closed form for special geometries (spherical wrist); fast, all solutions.
Numerical: iterate Δq = J⁺e from a guess; general, one nearby solution, can fail near singularities.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::07 Kinematics & Dynamics
notes.front: What is the manipulator Jacobian?
notes.back: The configuration-dependent matrix mapping joint velocities to end-effector twist: v = J(q)·q̇.
notes.analogy: A gear ratio that changes with posture: it tells you how fast the hand moves for each joint's speed right now.
notes.extra: Used for resolved-rate control, numerical inverse kinematics (IK), singularity/manipulability analysis and force mapping.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::07 Kinematics & Dynamics
notes.front: What is a kinematic singularity, and what happens near one?
notes.back: J(q) loses rank: the end-effector can't move in some direction (arm fully stretched, wrist axes aligned); nearby, small Cartesian motions demand huge joint velocities.
notes.source: Siciliano, Sciavicco, Villani & Oriolo, Robotics: Modelling, Planning and Control

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::07 Kinematics & Dynamics
notes.front: Standard numerical remedy near singularities?
notes.back: Damped least squares: q̇ = Jᵀ(JJᵀ + λ²I)⁻¹v, trading a little tracking error for bounded joint speeds.
notes.extra: Plus planning that keeps manipulability w = √det(JJᵀ) high.
notes.source: Siciliano, Sciavicco, Villani & Oriolo, Robotics: Modelling, Planning and Control

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::07 Kinematics & Dynamics
notes.front: Static force relationship between end-effector wrench and joint torques?
notes.back: τ = Jᵀ(q)·F (from power conservation τᵀq̇ = Fᵀv).
notes.extra: Uses: payload torque estimation, Cartesian impedance via joint torques, contact force from motor currents.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::07 Kinematics & Dynamics
notes.front: What is kinematic redundancy, and how is the null space used?
notes.back: More joints than task dimensions (7-DoF arm, 6-DoF pose). q̇ = J⁺v + (I − J⁺J)q̇0: the second term moves joints without moving the end-effector, for secondary goals (limits, obstacles, elbow posture).
notes.analogy: Keep your fingertip on a table and wiggle your elbow: the hand stays put while the arm reconfigures.
notes.source: Siciliano, Sciavicco, Villani & Oriolo, Robotics: Modelling, Planning and Control

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::07 Kinematics & Dynamics
notes.front: Manipulator equation of motion?
notes.back: M(q)q̈ + C(q,q̇)q̇ + g(q) = τ + Jᵀ(q)F<sub>ext</sub> — inertia, Coriolis/centrifugal, gravity, joint torques, external forces.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::07 Kinematics & Dynamics
notes.front: Inverse vs. forward dynamics: which is used for what?
notes.back:
Inverse (motion → torque, recursive Newton–Euler, O(n)): control.
Forward (torque → acceleration): simulation.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::07 Kinematics & Dynamics
notes.front: Differential drive: forward kinematics?
notes.back: v = (v<sub>r</sub> + v<sub>l</sub>)/2, ω = (v<sub>r</sub> − v<sub>l</sub>)/L (L = track width); ẋ = v cos θ, ẏ = v sin θ, θ̇ = ω.
notes.source: Siegwart, Nourbakhsh & Scaramuzza, Introduction to Autonomous Mobile Robots (2nd ed.)

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::07 Kinematics & Dynamics
notes.front: Differential drive: inverse kinematics (what a base controller does with cmd_vel)?
notes.back: v<sub>r,l</sub> = v ± ω·L/2.
notes.source: Siegwart, Nourbakhsh & Scaramuzza, Introduction to Autonomous Mobile Robots (2nd ed.)

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::07 Kinematics & Dynamics
notes.front: A differential-drive robot drives its wheels at equal speed in opposite directions. What motion results?
notes.back: v = 0 and ω = 2·v<sub>wheel</sub>/L: it spins in place about the centre of the axle.
notes.source: Siegwart, Nourbakhsh & Scaramuzza, Introduction to Autonomous Mobile Robots (2nd ed.)

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::07 Kinematics & Dynamics
notes.front: Why does wheel odometry drift without bound?
notes.back: Errors are integrated: slip, uneven floors, unequal wheel diameters, uncertain track width. Heading error dominates because it turns into position error with distance.
notes.analogy: Walking blindfolded counting steps: a 2° heading error barely matters after 5 m but puts you in the wrong street after 500 m.
notes.extra: Fix: calibrate systematic errors (UMBmark), fuse with inertial measurement unit (IMU), correct with exteroceptive localisation.
notes.source: Siegwart, Nourbakhsh & Scaramuzza, Introduction to Autonomous Mobile Robots (2nd ed.)

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::07 Kinematics & Dynamics
notes.front: Holonomic vs. non-holonomic mobile robots?
notes.back:
Non-holonomic: velocity constraint (diff-drive/car can't slide sideways) yet any pose is reachable by manoeuvring.
Holonomic: mecanum/omni bases command vx, vy, ω independently.
notes.analogy: Parallel parking: a car can't slide into the space but can still get there by manoeuvring.
notes.extra: Trade-off of omni rollers: less traction, efficiency and odometry accuracy.
notes.source: Siegwart, Nourbakhsh & Scaramuzza, Introduction to Autonomous Mobile Robots (2nd ed.)

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::07 Kinematics & Dynamics
notes.front: What is an underactuated system? Robotic examples?
notes.back: Fewer actuators than degrees of freedom (DoF), so control must exploit natural dynamics. E.g. cart-pole, Acrobot, quadrotor (4 inputs, 6 DoF), every legged robot (unactuated floating base).

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::07 Kinematics & Dynamics
notes.front: What is the Zero Moment Point (ZMP)?
notes.back: Ground point where the net horizontal moment of contact forces is zero (≈ centre of pressure). If it stays inside the support polygon, the foot doesn't tip.
notes.source: Siciliano, Sciavicco, Villani & Oriolo, Robotics: Modelling, Planning and Control

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::07 Kinematics & Dynamics
notes.front: How did classical humanoids (ASIMO) use the zero moment point (ZMP), and what replaced it?
notes.back: Planned center of mass (CoM) trajectories with the Linear Inverted Pendulum so the ZMP tracked the footsteps: stable but flat-footed. Modern robots use model predictive control (MPC)/WBC or reinforcement learning (RL) with dynamic contacts.
notes.source: Siciliano, Sciavicco, Villani & Oriolo, Robotics: Modelling, Planning and Control

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::07 Kinematics & Dynamics
notes.front: What is the floating-base model of a legged robot?
notes.back: State = 6-DoF unactuated base pose + n joints; M(q)v̇ + h = Sᵀτ + ΣJ<sub>c</sub>ᵀf<sub>c</sub>, with contact forces in friction cones. Locomotion = choosing contacts and forces to move the base.
notes.analogy: A swimmer can't push on nothing: the body only moves by pushing on the water, just as the base only moves through foot contacts.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::08 Perception & State Estimation
notes.front: Pinhole camera projection equations?
notes.back: u = f<sub>x</sub>·X/Z + c<sub>x</sub>, v = f<sub>y</sub>·Y/Z + c<sub>y</sub>. Full model x ~ K[R | t]X; depth Z is lost.
notes.source: Hartley & Zisserman, Multiple View Geometry (2nd ed.); OpenCV calibration docs

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::08 Perception & State Estimation
notes.front: What are the camera intrinsics (matrix K)?
