notes.back: Focal lengths in pixels (f<sub>x</sub>, f<sub>y</sub>) and principal point (c<sub>x</sub>, c<sub>y</sub>); extrinsics [R | t] give the camera pose.
notes.source: Hartley & Zisserman, Multiple View Geometry (2nd ed.); OpenCV calibration docs

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::08 Perception & State Estimation
notes.front: What does camera calibration estimate?
notes.back: Intrinsics (fx, fy, cx, cy) and lens distortion (radial k1–3, tangential p1,2), optionally extrinsics.
notes.source: Hartley & Zisserman, Multiple View Geometry (2nd ed.); OpenCV calibration docs

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::08 Perception & State Estimation
notes.front: How is camera calibration done in practice?
notes.back: Zhang's method: 15–30 checkerboard/ChArUco images at varied poses → cv2.calibrateCamera → reprojection error < ~0.5 px. Redo when focus or resolution changes.
notes.source: Hartley & Zisserman, Multiple View Geometry (2nd ed.); OpenCV calibration docs

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::08 Perception & State Estimation
notes.front: What is hand–eye calibration, and what equation does it solve?
notes.back: Finding the fixed camera↔robot transform so detections can be expressed in the base frame; move the arm through many poses viewing a target and solve AX = XB.
notes.extra: Eye-in-hand: camera-to-flange. Eye-to-hand: camera-to-base. cv2.calibrateHandEye.
notes.source: Hartley & Zisserman, Multiple View Geometry (2nd ed.); OpenCV calibration docs

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::08 Perception & State Estimation
notes.front: Stereo depth equation?
notes.back: Z = f·B / d (focal length in px, baseline, disparity in px).
notes.source: Hartley & Zisserman, Multiple View Geometry (2nd ed.); OpenCV calibration docs

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::08 Perception & State Estimation
notes.front: How does stereo depth error grow with range, and how do you improve far range?
notes.back: Quadratically: δZ ≈ Z²/(f·B)·δd. Wider baseline or longer focal length helps far range but raises the minimum range.
notes.analogy: Your two eyes judge depth well at arm's length, but a distant mountain could be 10 or 12 km away; the views barely differ.
notes.source: Hartley & Zisserman, Multiple View Geometry (2nd ed.); OpenCV calibration docs

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::08 Perception & State Estimation
notes.front: Classical feature-matching pipeline between images?
notes.back: Detect key-points → describe → match (nearest neighbour + ratio test) → reject outliers with random sample consensus (RANSAC).
notes.extra: Descriptors: scale-invariant feature transform (SIFT) (accurate, slow), ORB (binary, real-time, ORB-SLAM). Learned: SuperPoint + LightGlue.
notes.source: Hartley & Zisserman, Multiple View Geometry (2nd ed.); OpenCV calibration docs

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::08 Perception & State Estimation
notes.front: What does random sample consensus (RANSAC) do?
notes.back: Repeatedly fits a model (homography, essential matrix) to random minimal subsets and keeps the one with most inliers, so outlier matches don't corrupt the estimate.
notes.analogy: Polling small random groups to find the story most witnesses agree on, ignoring the liars.
notes.source: Hartley & Zisserman, Multiple View Geometry (2nd ed.); OpenCV calibration docs

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::08 Perception & State Estimation
notes.front: What are fiducial markers (AprilTag, ArUco) used for?
notes.back: Robustly detectable coded squares; with known size and intrinsics, one tag gives the full 6-DoF pose (PnP). Used for ground truth, docking, calibration, tracking.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::08 Perception & State Estimation
notes.front: Bayes filter: what are the two steps?
notes.back: Predict with the motion model (uncertainty grows), then update with the measurement likelihood (uncertainty shrinks): bel(x) = η·p(z|x)·bel⁻(x).
notes.analogy: Dead reckoning on a ship: guess where you've drifted, then sharpen the guess when a lighthouse comes into view.
notes.extra: Kalman filter = Gaussian beliefs; particle filter = samples; histogram filter = grid. Assumes Markov property.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::08 Perception & State Estimation
notes.front: Kalman filter predict step?
notes.back:
x̂⁻ = Ax̂ + Bu
P⁻ = APAᵀ + Q

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::08 Perception & State Estimation
notes.front: Kalman filter update step?
notes.back:
K = P⁻Hᵀ(HP⁻Hᵀ + R)⁻¹
x̂ = x̂⁻ + K(z − Hx̂⁻)
P = (I − KH)P⁻

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::08 Perception & State Estimation
notes.front: What does the Kalman gain do, and when is the Kalman filter (KF) optimal?
notes.back: K weights prediction vs. measurement by their uncertainties (Q process noise, R measurement noise). Optimal for linear systems with Gaussian noise.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::08 Perception & State Estimation
notes.front: In a Kalman filter (KF), how does the gain change if measurement noise R is very large, or process noise Q is very large?
notes.back:
Large R: small gain, trust the prediction.
Large Q: larger gain, trust the measurements (the model is unreliable).

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::08 Perception & State Estimation
notes.front: Extended Kalman filter (EKF) vs. unscented Kalman filter (UKF)?
notes.back:
EKF: linearise f, h with Jacobians at the estimate; cheap, can diverge if strongly non-linear.
UKF: push sigma points through the true functions; no Jacobians, usually more accurate.
notes.extra: Robot Operating System (ROS): robot_localization fuses odometry + inertial measurement unit (IMU) (+global navigation satellite system (GNSS)) with either.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::08 Perception & State Estimation
notes.front: How does a particle filter work?
notes.back: Belief = N weighted samples: move each with the noisy motion model → weight by measurement likelihood → resample by weight.
notes.analogy: A search party spread over a map: teams in places that match what they see get reinforced; the rest are called back.
notes.extra: + Multi-modal beliefs → global localisation, kidnapped robot. − Cost grows with state dimension.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::08 Perception & State Estimation
notes.front: Why can resampling in a particle filter hurt, and what is the symptom?
notes.back: Repeatedly copying high-weight particles collapses diversity (particle depletion), so the filter can lock onto a wrong hypothesis and not recover.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::08 Perception & State Estimation
notes.front: What is AMCL?
notes.back: Adaptive Monte Carlo Localization: particle-filter localisation of a 2D-LiDAR robot in a known occupancy map, adapting particle count (KLD sampling). Nav2's default localiser.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::08 Perception & State Estimation
notes.front: Simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM): what is it, and why is it hard?
notes.back: Estimating trajectory and map of an unknown environment at once: a chicken-and-egg problem with correlated errors, drifting odometry and risky data association.
notes.analogy: Drawing a map of a dark cave while using that same unfinished map to work out where you are.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::08 Perception & State Estimation
notes.front: Graph-based simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM): front-end vs. back-end?
notes.back:
Front-end: turns sensor data into constraints (odometry, scan matching, feature tracking, place recognition).
Back-end: non-linear least-squares over a pose graph (g2o, GTSAM, Ceres).

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::08 Perception & State Estimation
notes.front: What is loop closure, and what is its risk?
notes.back: Recognising a revisited place adds an edge that lets the optimiser cancel accumulated drift. A false loop closure wrecks the map → robust kernels and verification.
notes.analogy: Walking around a block and recognising your front door: you suddenly know how far off your step count was all along.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::08 Perception & State Estimation
notes.front: What is an occupancy grid map?
notes.back: A 2D (or 3D voxel, OctoMap) grid where each cell holds the probability of being occupied, updated per beam in log-odds so updates are additions.
notes.extra: Assumes independent cells and known poses. The map format behind Nav2 costmaps.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::08 Perception & State Estimation
notes.front: What is ICP (Iterative Closest Point)?
notes.back: Align two point clouds by repeating: match each point to its nearest neighbour → solve the best rigid transform (SVD) → apply, until convergence.
notes.extra: Core of light detection and ranging (LiDAR) odometry/scan matching. Variants: point-to-plane, generalized iterative closest point (GICP); alternative: normal distributions transform (NDT).

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::08 Perception & State Estimation
notes.front: Iterative closest point (ICP)'s main weakness?
notes.back: Needs a good initial guess; otherwise converges to a local minimum.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::08 Perception & State Estimation
notes.front: Monocular visual odometry: what is the scale problem?
notes.back: With one camera, translation is recovered only up to an unknown scale, and the scale drifts.
notes.analogy: From a single photo you can't tell a toy car up close from a real one far away.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::08 Perception & State Estimation
notes.front: What does Visual-Inertial Odometry add over visual odometry (VO)?
notes.back: Fusing an inertial measurement unit (IMU) makes metric scale and gravity direction observable and bridges fast motion/brief visual drop-outs.
notes.extra: Examples: VINS-Fusion, OpenVINS, ORB-SLAM3; principle behind augmented reality (AR)/VR headset tracking.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::08 Perception & State Estimation
notes.text: Vision tasks: {{c1::object detection}} = class + bounding box; {{c2::semantic segmentation}} = class per pixel, no identities; {{c3::instance segmentation}} = a separate mask per object; {{c4::6D pose estimation}} = 3D position + orientation of an object.
notes.extra: Examples: YOLO; Mask R-CNN / Segment Anything; FoundationPose (what classical grasp planning needs).
notes.source: Kawaharazuka et al. 2025, VLA Models for Robotics: A Review

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::08 Perception & State Estimation
notes.front: How have vision foundation models changed robot perception?
notes.back: Pre-trained encoders replace task-specific training: CLIP/SigLIP (open-vocabulary), DINOv2 (dense geometric features), SAM/Grounding DINO (promptable segmentation/detection), Depth Anything.
notes.extra: SigLIP + DINOv2 is the most common vision front-end of vision-language-action models (VLAs) (e.g. OpenVLA).
notes.source: Kawaharazuka et al. 2025, VLA Models for Robotics: A Review

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::08 Perception & State Estimation
notes.front: What is real-time kinematic (RTK) global navigation satellite system (GNSS) positioning?
notes.back: A base station (or Networked Transport of RTCM via Internet Protocol (NTRIP) service) streams carrier-phase corrections; the rover resolves integer ambiguities → centimetre accuracy instead of metres.
notes.extra: Needs open sky and a correction link. Standard for agricultural/outdoor robots and survey drones.
notes.source: Siegwart, Nourbakhsh & Scaramuzza, Introduction to Autonomous Mobile Robots (2nd ed.)

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::09 Motion Planning & Navigation
notes.text: Motion layers: a {{c1::path}} is a geometric collision-free curve q(s); a {{c2::trajectory}} adds timing q(t) within velocity/acceleration limits; {{c3::control}} tracks it with feedback.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::09 Motion Planning & Navigation
notes.front: Dijkstra vs. A*?
notes.back: Dijkstra expands by cost-so-far g(n): optimal but explores in all directions. A* expands by g(n) + h(n); with h = 0 it is Dijkstra.
notes.analogy: Dijkstra searches like a ripple in a pond; A* is a ripple stretched toward where you think the goal is.
notes.extra: Variants: Theta* (any-angle), D* Lite (re-planning), Hybrid-A* (car kinematics).

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::09 Motion Planning & Navigation
notes.front: When is A* guaranteed optimal?
notes.back: When the heuristic is admissible (never overestimates, e.g. Euclidean distance); if also consistent, no node is re-expanded.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::09 Motion Planning & Navigation
notes.front: What happens to A* if the heuristic overestimates the true remaining cost?
notes.back: It may return a suboptimal path, because it can skip a cheaper route that looked more expensive than it was. Admissibility prevents this.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::09 Motion Planning & Navigation
notes.front: Why do arm planners sample configuration space instead of gridding it?
notes.back: A grid has resolutionn cells (curse of dimensionality), and C-space obstacles have no explicit form; only a collision checker exists.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::09 Motion Planning & Navigation
notes.front: What does 'probabilistically complete' mean for sampling-based planners?
notes.back: If a solution exists, the probability of finding it → 1 with more samples; but they can't prove that none exists.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::09 Motion Planning & Navigation
notes.front: Probabilistic roadmap (PRM) vs. rapidly-exploring random tree (RRT)?
notes.back:
PRM: multi-query; build a roadmap of collision-free samples once, then graph-search it (static scenes).
RRT: single-query; grow a tree from the start toward random samples (RRT-Connect grows two).
notes.analogy: PRM builds a road network for a city you'll drive often; RRT sends out a vine that grows toward random points until it reaches the goal.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::09 Motion Planning & Navigation
notes.front: What does RRT* add to rapidly-exploring random tree (RRT)?
notes.back: Asymptotic optimality: new nodes choose the cheapest parent nearby and rewire neighbours through themselves, so path cost converges to the optimum.
notes.extra: Informed RRT*/BIT* converge faster. Library: Open Motion Planning Library (OMPL). Paths are still usually shortcut/smoothed.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::09 Motion Planning & Navigation
notes.front: How is a geometric path turned into a smooth joint trajectory?
notes.back: Time-parameterise under limits: trapezoidal (or jerk-limited S-curve) velocity profiles, cubic/quintic polynomials or splines, or time-optimal parameterisation (TOPP-RA, TOTG, Ruckig).

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::09 Motion Planning & Navigation
notes.front: Cubic vs. quintic polynomial between way-points?
notes.back: Cubic matches position + velocity at both ends; quintic also matches acceleration (smoother, no acceleration jumps).

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::09 Motion Planning & Navigation
notes.front: Mobile navigation: global planner vs. local planner?
notes.back:
Global: route over the whole map (A*, Smac Hybrid-A*), re-planned occasionally.
Local/controller: at 10–20+ Hz turns route + live sensor data into velocity commands, dodging dynamic obstacles.
notes.analogy: The global planner is the satnav route; the local planner is your hands on the wheel avoiding the cyclist.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::09 Motion Planning & Navigation
notes.front: What is a costmap's inflation layer?
notes.back: It pads obstacles by the robot radius with decaying cost, so the planner keeps a margin and can treat the robot as a point.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::09 Motion Planning & Navigation
notes.front: How does the Dynamic Window Approach (DWA) pick a command?
notes.back: Sample (v, ω) pairs reachable within one step given acceleration limits, forward-simulate each briefly, drop colliding ones, choose the best score (heading, clearance, speed).

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::09 Motion Planning & Navigation
notes.front: How does model predictive path integral (MPPI) control work?
notes.back: Sample thousands of noisy control sequences, roll them out through the model, and average them weighted by exp(−cost): a sampling-based model predictive control (MPC) that handles non-convex costs (widely used in Nav2).

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::09 Motion Planning & Navigation
notes.front: Pure pursuit: how does it compute steering?
notes.back: Pick a path point one look-ahead distance L<sub>d</sub> ahead and follow the arc through it: κ = 2y/L<sub>d</sub>², ω = v·κ.
notes.analogy: Like riding a bike by looking a few metres ahead on the road rather than at your front wheel.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::09 Motion Planning & Navigation
notes.front: Pure pursuit: effect of short vs. long look-ahead?
notes.back: Short → accurate but oscillatory; long → smooth but cuts corners. Often scaled with speed (Regulated Pure Pursuit).

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::09 Motion Planning & Navigation
notes.front: Artificial potential fields: idea and fatal flaw?
notes.back: Goal attracts, obstacles repel; follow the negative gradient (cheap, reactive). Flaw: local minima (U-shaped obstacles) and oscillation in corridors.
notes.analogy: A marble rolling downhill to the goal can get stuck in a dip on the way and never get out.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::09 Motion Planning & Navigation
notes.front: Behavior Trees: how do Sequence and Fallback nodes work?
notes.back: Tree ticked from the root; nodes return SUCCESS/FAILURE/RUNNING. Sequence runs children until one fails; Fallback tries children until one succeeds (built-in recovery).
notes.source: Colledanchise & Ögren, Behavior Trees in Robotics and AI

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::09 Motion Planning & Navigation
notes.front: Why have Behavior Trees displaced finite state machines (FSMs) for robot task logic?
notes.back: Modular reusable sub-trees, no transition explosion, and inherently reactive (conditions re-checked every tick).
notes.analogy: An FSM is a flowchart of rooms with doors between every pair; a BT is a to-do list with fallbacks you re-read from the top every second.
notes.extra: Nav2's navigator is a BT (BehaviorTree.CPP, extensible markup language (XML)).
notes.source: Colledanchise & Ögren, Behavior Trees in Robotics and AI

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::09 Motion Planning & Navigation
notes.front: Sampling-based planning vs. trajectory optimisation for manipulators?
notes.back:
Sampling (rapidly-exploring random tree (RRT)-Connect): global, won't get stuck in local minima, jerky paths.
Optimisation (CHOMP, TrajOpt, cuRobo): smooth and fast but local, depends on the initial guess.
notes.extra: Common combo: sample a seed, then optimise. task and motion planning (TAMP) adds a symbolic layer for long-horizon tasks.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::09 Motion Planning & Navigation
notes.front: What is force closure, and what does it reduce to for a parallel-jaw gripper?
notes.back: Contact forces within friction cones can resist any external wrench. For a parallel gripper: an antipodal grasp, contact normals opposed and inside each other's friction cones.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::09 Motion Planning & Navigation
notes.front: Classical vs. data-driven grasp planning?
notes.back: Classical needs an object model and pose. Data-driven nets (Dex-Net, GraspNet, Contact-GraspNet) predict grasps directly from depth/point clouds of unknown objects.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::10 ROS 2 & Simulation
notes.front: What is Robot Operating System (ROS), if not an operating system?
notes.back: Open-source middleware + tools + libraries: inter-process messaging, drivers, visualisation (RViz), logging, build tooling, navigation/manipulation/perception packages.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::10 ROS 2 & Simulation
notes.front: Status of Robot Operating System (ROS) 1, and what ROS 2 changed?
notes.back: ROS 1 (final: Noetic) reached end-of-life on 31 May 2025. ROS 2: no central master, built on Data Distribution Service (DDS), real-time and multi-robot capable, security, lifecycle nodes.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::10 ROS 2 & Simulation
notes.text: Robot Operating System (ROS) 2 primitives: a {{c1::topic}} is anonymous many-to-many publish/subscribe; a {{c2::service}} is a quick request/response; an {{c3::action}} is a long-running, pre-emptable goal with feedback and a result.
notes.analogy: Topic = radio broadcast; service = phone call; action = ordering a taxi with live tracking that you can cancel.
notes.extra: Examples: topic: sensor data, cmd_vel; action: navigate to pose. Nodes are the processes; parameters configure them.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::10 ROS 2 & Simulation
notes.front: In Robot Operating System (ROS) 2, which primitive fits 'navigate to this pose', and why?
notes.back: An action: the task is long-running, needs progress feedback and must be cancellable. A service is a quick request/response; a topic has no goal or result.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::10 ROS 2 & Simulation
notes.front: What is Data Distribution Service (DDS)'s role in Robot Operating System (ROS) 2?
notes.back: Industrial pub/sub standard providing automatic peer discovery (no master), Real-Time Publish-Subscribe (RTPS) over User Datagram Protocol (UDP), and rich quality of service (QoS).

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::10 ROS 2 & Simulation
notes.front: What is the RMW layer, and why is Zenoh notable?
notes.back: The Robot Operating System (ROS) Middleware (RMW) interface abstracts the vendor (Fast DDS, Cyclone DDS, Connext). rmw_zenoh is a non-DDS option that behaves better over Wi-Fi and wide area network (WAN).
notes.extra: ROS_DOMAIN_ID isolates robots on a shared network.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::10 ROS 2 & Simulation
notes.front: Key Robot Operating System (ROS) 2 quality of service (QoS) settings?
notes.back: Reliability (RELIABLE vs BEST_EFFORT for lossy sensor streams), durability (TRANSIENT_LOCAL gives late joiners the last message: maps, robot_description), history depth.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::10 ROS 2 & Simulation
notes.front: Classic Robot Operating System (ROS) 2 quality of service (QoS) pitfall?
notes.back: Incompatible QoS = silently no data, e.g. a RELIABLE subscriber won't match a BEST_EFFORT publisher. Check with ros2 topic info -v.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::10 ROS 2 & Simulation
notes.front: Robot Operating System (ROS) 2 release pattern, and which distro should a new project pick?
notes.back: A release every May; even years are 5-year long-term support (LTS) tied to an Ubuntu LTS. Pick the newest LTS your drivers already support.
notes.extra: Odd-year releases are non-LTS (~1.5 years of support); Rolling is the development branch.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::10 ROS 2 & Simulation
notes.front: ROS Enhancement Proposal (REP) 105: standard frame chain of a mobile robot?
notes.back: map → odom → base_link → sensor frames
notes.source: REP 105, Coordinate Frames for Mobile Platforms

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::10 ROS 2 & Simulation
notes.front: ROS Enhancement Proposal (REP) 105: who publishes odom → base_link vs. map → odom, and how do they behave?
notes.back:
odom→base_link: odometry/IMU fusion; smooth but drifts.
map→odom: localisation/SLAM; globally accurate but can jump.
notes.analogy: odom is your step-counting sense of position; map is the occasional glance at a street sign that corrects it.
notes.extra: base_link → sensors: static transforms from the Unified Robot Description Format (URDF) via robot_state_publisher. Conventions: x forward, y left, z up (REP 103).
notes.source: REP 105, Coordinate Frames for Mobile Platforms

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::10 ROS 2 & Simulation
notes.front: Why should a local obstacle-avoidance controller work in the odom frame rather than the map frame?
notes.back: odom → base_link is smooth and continuous, while the map → odom correction can jump when localisation updates, causing sudden velocity commands.
notes.source: REP 105, Coordinate Frames for Mobile Platforms

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::10 ROS 2 & Simulation
notes.front: What is a Unified Robot Description Format (URDF)?
notes.back: Extensible markup language (XML) robot description: a tree of links (visual, collision, inertial) connected by joints (type, axis, limits); xacro adds macros.
notes.extra: Consumers: robot_state_publisher, RViz, MoveIt, ros2_control, simulators.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::10 ROS 2 & Simulation
notes.front: Unified Robot Description Format (URDF) limitations, and richer alternatives?
notes.back: Tree only (no closed loops), one robot. Richer: Gazebo Simulation Description Format (SDF), MuJoCo MJCF, OpenUSD (Isaac Sim).

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::10 ROS 2 & Simulation
notes.front: What is ros2_control?
notes.back: Robot Operating System (ROS) 2's real-time control framework: hardware interface plugins expose state/command interfaces; a controller manager runs read → update → write; swappable controllers (joint_trajectory, diff_drive …).
notes.analogy: Like a device-driver model: controllers talk to an abstract interface, so swapping sim for hardware is a plugin change.
notes.extra: The same controllers run on Gazebo, a mock system or the real robot; MoveIt and Nav2 sit on top.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::10 ROS 2 & Simulation
notes.text: Nav2: the {{c1::BT Navigator}} orchestrates the task; the {{c2::planner server}} computes the global path; the {{c3::controller server}} follows it; the {{c4::behaviour server}} runs recoveries (spin, back up, wait).
notes.extra: Also: global/local costmaps, adaptive Monte Carlo localization (AMCL) + map server or simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM) Toolbox, smoother, waypoint follower, collision monitor, lifecycle manager.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::10 ROS 2 & Simulation
notes.front: What does MoveIt 2 provide?
notes.back: Robot Operating System (ROS) 2 manipulation framework: planning scene + collision checking, motion-planning plugins (Open Motion Planning Library (OMPL), Pilz, STOMP), inverse kinematics (IK) plugins (KDL, TRAC-IK), time parameterisation, execution via ros2_control.
notes.extra: Also: MoveIt Servo (real-time jogging/tele-op), Task Constructor (multi-stage pick-and-place).

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::10 ROS 2 & Simulation
notes.front: What is micro-ROS?
notes.back: Robot Operating System (ROS) 2 for microcontrollers (rclc on Micro XRCE-DDS, on FreeRTOS/Zephyr/bare-metal); an agent on the Linux host bridges the microcontroller unit (MCU) into the ROS 2 graph as a first-class node.
notes.extra: Targets: ESP32, STM32, Teensy, Pico, over serial/USB/UDP/CAN.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::10 ROS 2 & Simulation
notes.front: What is rosbag2, and why is it central to development?
notes.back: Records and replays topics with timestamps (ros2 bag record/play, MCAP format): offline debugging, repeatable tuning on identical data, regression tests, datasets.
notes.analogy: A flight recorder you can replay into the software as if the flight were happening again.
notes.extra: Visualise with RViz, Foxglove, PlotJuggler; replay with use_sim_time.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::10 ROS 2 & Simulation
notes.front: Gazebo vs. MuJoCo: what is each best at?
notes.back:
Gazebo (modern gz): Robot Operating System (ROS)-integrated full-system and navigation testing with sensors and worlds.
MuJoCo: fast, accurate contact dynamics; research standard for control and reinforcement learning (RL).
notes.extra: Gazebo Classic is end-of-life; use modern gz. MuJoCo GPU variants: MJX, MuJoCo Warp.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::10 ROS 2 & Simulation
notes.front: GPU-parallel robot-learning simulators vs a classic Robot Operating System (ROS) simulator: what distinguishes them?
notes.back: Physics (and often rendering) run on the GPU, so thousands of environments step in parallel for reinforcement learning (RL) and synthetic data; some are differentiable. Classic simulators (Gazebo) favour ROS integration and full-system testing over throughput.
notes.extra: Examples: Isaac Sim/Lab (PhysX, photoreal OpenUSD rendering), Newton (open-source differentiable physics on Warp), MuJoCo MJX/Warp, Genesis.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::11 Robot Learning
notes.front: Markov Decision Process: components and goal?
notes.back: (S, A, P, R, γ): states, actions, transitions P(s′|s,a), reward, discount. Goal: a policy π(a|s) maximising expected discounted return Σγ<sup>t</sup>r<sub>t</sub>.
notes.source: Sutton & Barto, Reinforcement Learning: An Introduction (2nd ed.)

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::11 Robot Learning
notes.front: Why are real robots partially observable Markov decision processes (POMDPs), and how do policies cope?
notes.back: They never see the true state, only images and joint readings. Remedies: feed an observation history, recurrent/transformer memory, or an estimated state.
notes.source: Sutton & Barto, Reinforcement Learning: An Introduction (2nd ed.)

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::11 Robot Learning
notes.front: Reinforcement learning (RL) vs. imitation learning for robots: core trade-off?
notes.back:
RL: learns from reward; can exceed humans, but sample-hungry and unsafe → mostly in sim.
IL: supervised from demos; no reward/sim needed, but bounded by demo quality and coverage.
notes.extra: Frontier practice: pre-train by imitation, improve with RL.
notes.source: Sutton & Barto, Reinforcement Learning: An Introduction (2nd ed.)

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::11 Robot Learning
notes.front: Which learning paradigm dominates locomotion, and which manipulation?
notes.back: Locomotion: reinforcement learning (RL) in simulation (dynamics are simulable, rewards easy). Manipulation: imitation learning from real demonstrations (contact and visuals are hard to simulate).
notes.source: Sutton & Barto, Reinforcement Learning: An Introduction (2nd ed.)

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::11 Robot Learning
notes.front: What is Behaviour Cloning's fundamental failure mode?
notes.back: Compounding error / covariate shift: small mistakes lead to states the expert never visited, where the policy is worse; error grows ~O(T²) with horizon.
notes.analogy: A learner driver who only ever watched perfect driving: once slightly off the lane, they've never seen how to get back.
notes.extra: Mitigations: recovery data, dataset aggregation (DAgger), action chunking, noise injection, diffusion/flow policies.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::11 Robot Learning
notes.front: How does dataset aggregation (DAgger) fix behaviour cloning's distribution shift?
notes.back: Run the learner's policy, have the expert label the states it visits, add them and retrain. Training data matches the learner's own states → error grows linearly, not quadratically.
notes.analogy: A driving instructor grabbing the wheel exactly where you go wrong, and those moments becoming the lesson.
notes.extra: Robotics variant: HG-DAgger, where the operator takes over only when failure looms; those corrections become data.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::11 Robot Learning
notes.front: Proximal policy optimization (PPO): what is it, and where is it used in robotics?
notes.back: On-policy policy gradient with a clipped surrogate objective limiting each update; stable and scales across thousands of parallel sims → standard for sim-trained locomotion.
notes.source: Schulman et al. 2017, PPO · Haarnoja et al. 2018, SAC

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::11 Robot Learning
notes.front: Soft actor-critic (SAC): what is it, and where is it preferred?
notes.back: Off-policy actor-critic with a replay buffer and an entropy bonus; far more sample-efficient → preferred for learning directly on real robots.
notes.source: Schulman et al. 2017, PPO · Haarnoja et al. 2018, SAC

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::11 Robot Learning
notes.front: Reward shaping vs. reward hacking?
notes.back:
Shaping: adding dense intermediate terms because sparse rewards make exploration hopeless (locomotion: 10–20 terms).
Hacking: maximising the written reward in an unintended way (vibrating forward, exploiting sim bugs).
notes.analogy: Hacking is the cobra effect: pay per dead cobra and people start breeding cobras.
notes.extra: Alternatives: motion-imitation rewards from mocap, learned reward models, sparse reward + demos.
notes.source: Sutton & Barto, Reinforcement Learning: An Introduction (2nd ed.)

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::11 Robot Learning
notes.front: Where does the sim-to-real gap come from?
notes.back: Simulator errors in dynamics (friction, contact), actuators (backlash, bandwidth, latency), sensing (noise, delay) and visuals (rendering vs. real cameras).
notes.extra: Remedies: system identification, domain randomisation, learned actuator models, online adaptation, real-world fine-tuning.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::11 Robot Learning
notes.front: What is domain randomisation, and why does it enable sim-to-real transfer?
notes.back: Randomise physics (mass, friction, motor strength, delays, pushes) and/or visuals every episode, so the real world looks like just another sample and the policy must be robust.
notes.analogy: Training a pilot in a hundred slightly different simulators so the real plane feels like one more variant.
notes.extra: Too little → no transfer; too much → over-conservative. Main reason reinforcement learning (RL) locomotion transfers zero-shot.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::11 Robot Learning
notes.front: What goes wrong if domain randomisation ranges are too wide?
notes.back: The policy becomes overly conservative or fails to learn, since it must handle conditions no real robot will meet. Ranges should cover the plausible real-world uncertainty.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::11 Robot Learning
notes.front: What is an actuator network, and why did it matter for legged reinforcement learning (RL)?
notes.back: A small net trained on hardware logs to predict the torque an actuator actually produces from recent commands/states (capturing friction, compliance, delay). Put into the sim, it closed the sim-to-real gap for ANYmal.
notes.source: Hwangbo et al. 2019, Learning agile and dynamic motor skills for legged robots (Science Robotics)

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::11 Robot Learning
notes.front: Teacher–student (privileged) learning: how does it work?
notes.back: Teacher: reinforcement learning (RL) in sim with privileged info (friction, height map, contacts). Student: on-board sensors only, trained by supervision to imitate the teacher or infer the privileged latent from proprioceptive history.
notes.analogy: A sighted guide teaches a blindfolded student; the student learns to infer the terrain from how their feet feel.
notes.source: Kumar et al. 2021, RMA: Rapid Motor Adaptation

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::11 Robot Learning
notes.front: What is Rapid Motor Adaptation (RMA)?
notes.back: A base policy conditioned on an 'extrinsics' latent plus an adaptation module estimating it online from recent states/actions → adapts to new terrain/payloads in fractions of a second, no real-world fine-tuning.
notes.source: Kumar et al. 2021, RMA: Rapid Motor Adaptation

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::11 Robot Learning
notes.front: Why did massively parallel GPU simulation change robot reinforcement learning (RL)?
notes.back: Physics and network both run on the GPU, so thousands of environments step in parallel without CPU–GPU transfer; quadruped walking trained in minutes on one GPU (Rudin et al. 2021).
notes.extra: Tools: Isaac Lab, MuJoCo MJX/Warp, Genesis, ManiSkill. A terrain curriculum raises difficulty automatically.
notes.source: Rudin et al. 2021, Learning to Walk in Minutes

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::11 Robot Learning
notes.front: What is action chunking (ACT)?
notes.back: The policy predicts the next k actions (e.g. 50–100 at 50 Hz) per inference instead of one.
notes.analogy: Writing in whole words rather than letter by letter: fewer decisions, smoother strokes.
notes.extra: ACT adds a conditional variational autoencoder (VAE) and temporal ensembling of overlapping chunks. Introduced with ALOHA; now used by virtually all vision-language-action models (VLAs).
notes.source: Zhao et al. 2023, ALOHA / Action Chunking with Transformers

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::11 Robot Learning
notes.front: Why does action chunking help imitation learning?
notes.back: Shorter effective decision horizon → less compounding error; copes with non-Markovian demo quirks (pauses); smoother motion.
notes.source: Zhao et al. 2023, ALOHA / Action Chunking with Transformers

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::11 Robot Learning
notes.front: What is the downside of executing very long action chunks?
notes.back: Less reactivity: the robot commits to many steps without new observations, so disturbances or failures are noticed late.
notes.source: Zhao et al. 2023, ALOHA / Action Chunking with Transformers

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::11 Robot Learning
notes.front: How does Diffusion Policy generate actions?
notes.back: Iteratively denoises Gaussian noise into an action sequence, conditioned on recent observations; executes part, then re-plans (receding horizon).

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::11 Robot Learning
notes.front: Which behaviour-cloning problem does Diffusion Policy solve?
notes.back: Multi-modality: demos solve the task in different ways (left or right). Regression averages the modes into an invalid action; a diffusion model represents the distribution and commits to one.
notes.analogy: Averaging 'swerve left' and 'swerve right' gives 'drive straight into the tree'.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::11 Robot Learning
notes.front: Main ways to collect manipulation demonstrations?
notes.back:
• Leader–follower tele-op (ALOHA, GELLO, SO-101)
  • virtual reality (VR)/hand tracking (standard for humanoids)
  • Hand-held grippers (Universal Manipulation Interface (UMI); trajectories via visual simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM))
  • Egocentric human video: most scalable, no action labels
notes.extra: Quality, diversity and recovery examples matter more than sheer volume.
notes.source: Kawaharazuka et al. 2025, VLA Models for Robotics: A Review

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::12 Physical AI & Foundation Models
notes.front: What is 'Physical AI' / embodied AI?
notes.back: AI that perceives, reasons and acts in the physical world through a body, closing the loop from raw sensors to motor commands under real physics, timing and safety constraints.
notes.extra: Current paradigm: foundation models (vision-language-action models (VLAs), world models) + sim/synthetic data + fleet data, replacing hand-built pipelines for unstructured tasks.
notes.source: NVIDIA 2025, Cosmos World Foundation Model Platform for Physical AI

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::12 Physical AI & Foundation Models
notes.front: What is Moravec's paradox, and its consequence for robotics today?
notes.back: High-level reasoning is easy for computers, while a one-year-old's perception and mobility are hard. Sensorimotor skill is unconscious and evolved, and no internet-scale robot-action dataset exists: the central bottleneck.
notes.analogy: Chess is the tip of the iceberg we can see; picking up the chess piece is the huge part underwater.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::12 Physical AI & Foundation Models
notes.front: What is a Vision-Language-Action (VLA) model?
notes.back: A model taking images + a language instruction (optionally proprioception) and directly outputting robot actions, usually a pre-trained vision-language model (VLM) backbone plus an action head (tokens or diffusion/flow).
notes.extra: Systems where an LLM merely picks pre-trained skills (SayCan) are not VLAs.
notes.source: Kawaharazuka et al. 2025, VLA Models for Robotics: A Review

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::12 Physical AI & Foundation Models
notes.front: RT-1 vs. RT-2: what was RT-2's key idea?
notes.back: RT-1 trained from scratch on robot data only. RT-2 wrote actions as text tokens and co-fine-tuned a web-pre-trained vision-language model (VLM) on web + robot data, so web knowledge transferred to control.
notes.extra: Result: semantic generalisation absent from robot data ('pick up the extinct animal'). It coined the term vision-language-action (VLA).

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::12 Physical AI & Foundation Models
notes.front: How do autoregressive vision-language-action models (VLAs) (RT-2, OpenVLA) tokenise actions, and what is the drawback?
notes.back: Each action dimension per step is binned into 256 tokens. At high control rates that yields many correlated tokens → slow inference, poor dexterous learning.
notes.source: Pertsch et al. 2025, FAST action tokenizer

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::12 Physical AI & Foundation Models
notes.front: What does the FAST action tokenizer change?
notes.back: Applies a discrete cosine transform (DCT) to each action chunk, quantises, then compresses with byte-pair encoding (BPE) → far fewer tokens, ~5× faster training, and autoregressive vision-language-action models (VLAs) that match diffusion-style models on dexterous tasks.
notes.analogy: Like JPEG for motion: store the few frequencies that matter instead of every sample.
notes.source: Pertsch et al. 2025, FAST action tokenizer

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::12 Physical AI & Foundation Models
notes.front: What is Open X-Embodiment (OXE), and what did it show?
notes.back: A pooled dataset of 60 robot datasets (1M+ trajectories, 22 embodiments). One policy trained on the mix outperformed each lab's own-data policy: positive cross-embodiment transfer.
notes.extra: Default pre-training corpus for Octo/OpenVLA. Open issue: differing action spaces, cameras and rates.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::12 Physical AI & Foundation Models
notes.front: OpenVLA: architecture and significance?
notes.back: 7B open vision-language-action (VLA): Llama 2 + fused SigLIP + DINOv2 encoders, 256-bin action tokens, trained on Open X-Embodiment (OXE). Beat the closed 55B RT-2-X and showed cheap low-rank adaptation (LoRA) fine-tuning on consumer GPUs.
notes.extra: Follow-up OpenVLA-OFT: parallel decoding of continuous action chunks, much faster.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::12 Physical AI & Foundation Models
notes.front: π0 (Physical Intelligence): what is the architecture?
notes.back: A pre-trained vision-language model (VLM) (PaliGemma ~3B) plus a ~300M action expert that generates continuous action chunks by flow matching, enabling ~50 Hz dexterous control.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::12 Physical AI & Foundation Models
notes.front: π0's training recipe borrowed from LLMs?
notes.back: Pre-train on large, diverse cross-embodiment data (~10 000 h), then post-train on smaller high-quality task data.
notes.analogy: Like an LLM's pre-training then instruction tuning: broad competence first, polished behaviour second.
notes.extra: Weights open-sourced (openpi).

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::12 Physical AI & Foundation Models
notes.front: Flow matching vs. diffusion for action generation?
notes.back: Diffusion reverses a stochastic noising process over many steps. Flow matching regresses a velocity field moving noise to data along near-straight paths; inference integrates an ordinary differential equation (ODE) in ~5–10 steps → low latency.
notes.analogy: Diffusion is finding your way down a foggy mountain step by step; flow matching is learning the direct ski run.
notes.extra: Used by π0, GR00T N1 and successors.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::12 Physical AI & Foundation Models
notes.front: System 1 / System 2 vision-language-action (VLA) architecture: what does each part do?
notes.back:
System 2: large vision-language model (VLM) reasoning slowly (few Hz), emitting a latent conditioning.
System 1: small fast visuomotor policy turning it + fresh observations into actions at control rate (e.g. 200 Hz).
notes.analogy: A rally co-driver reading pace notes (slow, deliberate) while the driver's hands react instantly to the road.
notes.extra: Examples: Figure Helix (S2 ~7B at 7–9 Hz, S1 ~80M at 200 Hz); NVIDIA GR00T N1.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::12 Physical AI & Foundation Models
notes.front: Which trade-off does the dual-system vision-language-action (VLA) resolve?
notes.back: 'General but slow' (big vision-language model (VLM)) vs. 'fast but narrow' (small policy): each runs at its natural rate, asynchronously.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::12 Physical AI & Foundation Models
notes.front: Three-tier vision-language-action (VLA) hierarchy: what is a 'System 0' layer?
notes.back: A small (~10M-parameter) network at ~1 kHz mapping full-body state to joint commands: a learned whole-body controller for balance and contact, typically trained in simulation to track reference motion.
notes.extra: Pattern: a pixels-to-torque hierarchy (S2 reasoning → S1 at ~200 Hz → S0 at 1 kHz), each layer at its natural time-scale. Example: Figure's Helix 02.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::12 Physical AI & Foundation Models
notes.front: π0.5: what did it add over π0, and how?
notes.back: Open-world generalisation (cleaning unseen homes) via co-training on heterogeneous data (many robots, web data, verbal instructions) and hierarchical inference: predict a language sub-task, then the action chunk.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::12 Physical AI & Foundation Models
notes.front: π0.7 (2026): what is 'diverse context conditioning'?
notes.back: Training prompts describe not just what to do but how: episode metadata on data quality/strategy and sub-goal images.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::12 Physical AI & Foundation Models
notes.front: Why does diverse context conditioning help (π0.7)?
notes.back: It disambiguates mixed-quality data, so the model can learn from demos, failed roll-outs and non-robot data, then be steered at test time toward fast, high-quality behaviour.
notes.analogy: Labelling practice recordings 'beginner, sloppy' vs. 'expert, clean' lets you learn from all of them and then ask for the expert version.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::12 Physical AI & Foundation Models
notes.front: What training recipe do open humanoid foundation policies (e.g. NVIDIA GR00T N) follow?
notes.back: A vision-language model (VLM) 'System 2' plus a diffusion-transformer/flow 'System 1', trained cross-embodiment on real tele-op, human video (latent actions) and synthetic data, then post-trained per robot.
notes.source: NVIDIA Isaac GR00T · GR00T N1 paper

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::12 Physical AI & Foundation Models
notes.front: Orchestrator–executor split in robot foundation models: what does each model do?
notes.back:
Orchestrator: an embodied-reasoning vision-language model (VLM) that plans, points at targets and checks progress.
Executor: the VLA that carries out each step.
notes.extra: Example: Gemini Robotics-ER 1.5 (orchestrator) + Gemini Robotics 1.5 (VLA).

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::12 Physical AI & Foundation Models
notes.front: What are motion transfer and 'thinking before acting' in vision-language-action models (VLAs)?
notes.back:
Motion Transfer: learning from multi-embodiment data so skills transfer across robots without robot-specific post-training.
Thinking before acting: the VLA interleaves language reasoning with actions (embodied chain-of-thought).
notes.extra: Example: both are headline features of Gemini Robotics 1.5.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::12 Physical AI & Foundation Models
notes.front: What is a world (foundation) model in Physical AI?
notes.back: A generative model predicting future observations (usually video) from the current one and ideally actions: a learned simulator of visual physics (e.g. NVIDIA Cosmos).
notes.analogy: Imagination for a robot: picturing what happens if it pushes the cup before actually doing it.
notes.source: NVIDIA 2025, Cosmos World Foundation Model Platform for Physical AI

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::12 Physical AI & Foundation Models
notes.front: Uses and main limitation of world models?
notes.back: Uses: synthetic data, policy evaluation in imagination, planning/model-based control, representation pre-training. Limitation: long-horizon physical and action-conditional consistency.
notes.source: NVIDIA 2025, Cosmos World Foundation Model Platform for Physical AI

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::12 Physical AI & Foundation Models
notes.front: What is the 2026 trend toward 'world-action models'?
notes.back: Start from a pre-trained video generation model (which already encodes dynamics) and train it to predict future frames and actions jointly, instead of adding an action head to a vision-language model (VLM).
notes.extra: Why: video carries motion priors image–text lacks; imagined futures enable planning. Open issue: inference cost at control rate.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::12 Physical AI & Foundation Models
notes.front: Robot data pyramid: what are the three tiers, from scarce to abundant?
notes.back: Real tele-operation (best signal, costly) → simulation/synthetic (unlimited, sim-to-real gap) → human video (vast, no action labels). Plus web image–text via the vision-language model (VLM) backbone.
notes.extra: Example: NVIDIA reported ~40% gain for GR00T N1 by adding synthetic trajectories to real data.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::12 Physical AI & Foundation Models
notes.front: How can policies learn from human video that has no action labels?
notes.back: Latent action models (e.g. LAPA): a vector quantization (VQ)-VAE infers a discrete 'latent action' between frames; pre-train on those, then swap in a real action head. Also hand-pose retargeting.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::12 Physical AI & Foundation Models
notes.front: Why apply reinforcement learning (RL) to large vision-language-action models (VLAs), and how is the big backbone protected?
notes.back: Imitation plateaus below production reliability and speed; RL learns from the policy's own experience. Often RL acts only on a small head or the noise space (DSRL), keeping the backbone frozen.
notes.extra: Examples: hardware-in-the-loop (HIL)-SERL with human corrections; Physical Intelligence's π*0.6/RECAP (advantage-conditioned training on autonomous roll-outs).

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::12 Physical AI & Foundation Models
notes.front: A vision-language-action (VLA) needs ~100 ms per inference but the robot must move smoothly at 50 Hz. Main techniques?
notes.back: Action chunking (~1 s per inference), asynchronous inference (next chunk computed while the current runs), and Real-Time Chunking.
notes.extra: Also: few-step flow matching, small System-1 nets, quantisation/TensorRT.
notes.source: Kawaharazuka et al. 2025, VLA Models for Robotics: A Review

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::12 Physical AI & Foundation Models
notes.front: What is Real-Time Chunking (RTC)?
notes.back: Actions that will already have executed by the time inference finishes are treated as frozen, and the rest of the new chunk is 'inpainted' to match them → no pauses or jerks at chunk boundaries.
notes.analogy: Laying new track ahead of a moving train, joined smoothly to the section it's already on.
notes.source: Kawaharazuka et al. 2025, VLA Models for Robotics: A Review

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::12 Physical AI & Foundation Models
notes.front: Why is evaluating generalist robot policies hard?
notes.back: Real-world trials are slow, noisy, lab-specific and not reproducible; success depends on unreported details. Treat launch-day claims with caution.
notes.source: Kawaharazuka et al. 2025, VLA Models for Robotics: A Review

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::12 Physical AI & Foundation Models
notes.front: Benchmarks for generalist robot policies: sim vs. real-world?
notes.back:
Sim: LIBERO (near-saturated), CALVIN, SimplerEnv, RoboCasa, ManiSkill.
Real: RoboArena, crowd-sourced pairwise comparisons on the standard DROID platform across labs.
notes.source: Kawaharazuka et al. 2025, VLA Models for Robotics: A Review

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::12 Physical AI & Foundation Models
notes.front: How can a hobbyist get hands-on with Physical AI for a few hundred euros?
notes.back: LeRobot (Hugging Face: datasets, tele-op tools, action chunking transformer (ACT)/Diffusion/π0/SmolVLA) + an SO-101 leader/follower arm pair (~€100–250).
notes.extra: Workflow: ~50 tele-op demos → dataset on the Hub → train ACT or fine-tune SmolVLA (~450M, consumer GPU) → run on the arm.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::12 Physical AI & Foundation Models
notes.front: Main argument for humanoid robots?
notes.back: The world (stairs, doors, tools) is built for the human form, so one body can do many jobs, and human-shaped robots can learn from human data (tele-op retargeting, mocap, egocentric video).

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::12 Physical AI & Foundation Models
notes.front: Main counter-arguments to humanoids?
notes.back: Legs add cost, energy and fall risk where wheels suffice; dexterous hands/touch are the bottleneck; reliability far below industrial 99.9%+; safety certification near people unresolved.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::12 Physical AI & Foundation Models
notes.front: Why does a learned policy still need independent low-level safety, and what does it include?
notes.back: A neural policy has no guarantees, so safety is enforced around it: e-stop, torque/speed/workspace limits, collision detection, watchdogs and command timeouts, independent of the AI.
notes.analogy: A circuit breaker doesn't trust the appliance: it trips whatever the appliance thinks it is doing.

notes.deck: Robotics: Arduino to Physical AI::12 Physical AI & Foundation Models
notes.front: Safety layers above the hardware for learned robot policies?
notes.back: Standards: ISO 10218 / ISO/TS 15066 (power-and-force limiting, speed-and-separation). Control: impedance control, control barrier function (CBF)/MPC safety filters. Semantic: reasoning about hazards (ASIMOV benchmark), oversight, staged deployment.
